title: Penalty corners take center stage as Penn State field hockey beats Delaware for 3rd straight win
author: Owen Lomotan I The Daily Collegian
description:
Following their 2-0 home win over Villanova on Friday, Penn State field hockey aimed to make it three straight victories against the Delaware Blue Hens on Sunday.

The Nittany Lions did just that with a 2-1 victory; however, the win was defined by more than the final score. Penalty corners became the biggest factor in the game's flow, giving Penn State repeated opportunities to generate offense while also forcing its defense to withstand the Blue Hen attack.

Penn State was awarded three penalty corners in the first quarter, with two taken by junior forward Ella Gaitan and another by sophomore defensive back Lilly Holmes. None found the back of the net, but the early opportunities established a pattern that continued throughout the afternoon.

With 13 minutes left in the second quarter, Gaitan finally converted one of those opportunities, giving Penn State a 1-0 lead. The Nittany Lions earned two more penalty corners before halftime, taken by Gaitan and sophomore forward Joji Purdy.

Gaitan's goal remained the only score before halftime, but Penn State's ability to create chances from penalty corners helped keep pressure on Delaware. The Nittany Lions also limited the Blue Hens to just two penalty corners in the opening half.

Delaware came out of halftime with a response. Junior goalkeeper Aby Deverka blocked a shot just 45 seconds into the third quarter, but the Blue Hens eventually found the tying goal through fifth-year midfielder Alexa Michielsen with just under 14 minutes remaining.

For Deverka, the key was remaining composed after giving up the goal.

“Just knowing that my teammates expect something of me and I expect something of myself,” Deverka said. “Just staying grounded with that, staying composed. When I had that one goal against, I was immediately okay, next one, so what can I do to help us with this game.”

Penn State's penalty-corner opportunities continued to provide an answer. After another chance by Holmes came up empty, Gaitan found the net again with 12:14 remaining in the third quarter, giving the Nittany Lions a 2-1 lead.

The goal proved to be the difference.

Delaware continued to challenge Penn State defensively and earned several penalty corners of its own, but Deverka and the Nittany Lion defense repeatedly prevented those opportunities from becoming goals.

Within the last 10 minutes of regulation, both teams were awarded two penalty corners. On the defensive end, Deverka and sophomore defensive back Cooper Cutchins came up with crucial blocks inside the circle. On the offensive end, Gaitan and Purdy were unable to convert their opportunities, leaving Penn State with its one-goal advantage.

“We knew that Delaware was just a very competitive program, it’s a new team this year. We didn’t know a lot going into them,”Deverka said. “We saw that they beat No.18 Monmouth, and we’re like okay, we need to put respect on their name. Just going into this, we had our gameplan and we just stuck to it.”

Coach Hannah Prince emphasized the importance of players like Deverka making those late-game plays.

“[Deverka] got recognition after our last game for our hard hat hero award just for being really solid with her intensity, with her presence, stepping up in clutch moments so can’t say enough good things,” Prince said. “[Deverka] works her butt off, she demands from her teammates, she’s just one of those kids that isn’t afraid to say the hard things that is hard to hear but is inevitably going to help us.”

The win gives Penn State three straight victories and provides another example of how the Nittany Lions can use penalty corners to create opportunities while relying on their defense to protect narrow leads.

Penn State will now welcome No. 2 Princeton to Happy Valley at noon on Sept. 13.

“I think for the first couple days, we’re gonna focus really on us,” Prince said. “Having a full week before our next game allows us the opportunity to really go back to the drawing board of what we need to do first and then the adjustments we need to see in our own play regardless of our opponent.”

For the Nittany Lions, the focus heading into the week will remain on improving the details of their game while maintaining the identity that has helped them win three straight.

“There’s the X’s and Os, and there’s the fitness component and the penalty corner component of the game, but to us, being true to our values, staying humble, being a blue-collar team,” Prince said. “This year, we’re an underdog; we’re not ranked, but we have the ability to compete with any team in the country.”

Up Next

The Nittany Lions return to action at home next Sunday with Youth Day & Alumni Day, as they host Princeton. Start time is slated for noon.

title: Week 1 report card | Penn State’s offense produces success, defense generates shutout against Marshall
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s season opened on Saturday with a shutout victory over Marshall, starting Matt Campbell’s tenure off on the right foot.

Between a dominant performance from wide receivers to Rocco Becht’s debut in Beaver Stadium, the Nittany Lions had a strong showing across the board.

Here’s how I’d grade the different aspects of Penn State’s game in Week 1.

Overall grade: A-

Coaching staff: A

Campbell’s Penn State debut couldn’t have gone much better. He became the first Penn State coach with a shutout in their first game since 1915 and made a pair of fourth down conversion calls that proved fruitful.

The coordinators and assistant coaches also made the most of their available players with several depth players unavailable. They were able to play a bunch of different guys, giving them meaningful reps.

Offense: B+

Against a Sun Belt conference opponent, the Nittany Lions succeeded with the passing game alone. However, the run game was a major issue that was never able to develop.

Quarterbacks: A-

If this rating was on Becht alone, it would be an “A.” His Penn State debut produced 271 passing yards and four touchdowns with no turnovers.

In relief, Alex Manske was solid with a 75% completion percentage. Connor Barry, meanwhile, had two of his three plays go backwards.

Passing game: A

The lack of contributions from the tight ends, as Benjamin Brahmer and Andrew Rappleyea recorded just one catch each, might’ve decreased this grade any other week, but the absolute dominant performance from the wide receivers helped keep the “A” rating.

Koby Howard’s performance was lights out, tallying 161 yards and a touchdown. Combined with touchdowns from Brett Eskildsen and Zay Robinson, the Nittany Lions’ passing game flourished.

Rushing game: C+

The rushing game was arguably the worst aspect of Saturday’s performance for the Nittany Lions. The two leading running backs, Carson Hansen and James Peoples, didn’t find the end zone, while Quinton Martin Jr. and Cam Wallace did score as Penn State ran the clock out.

The Nittany Lions averaged 3.6 yards per carry on the ground.

Offensive line: A-

Becht had all the time in the world on numerous drives, including Howard’s first collegiate touchdown, and allowed just one sack all game.

Defense: A

Penn State’s defense kept Marshall off the board for 60 minutes, which was a testament to D’Anton Lynn’s playcalling.

The other reason for celebration was the lack of big plays from the Thundering Herd. Their biggest rush was for 10 yards, while their longest reception went for 14 yards.

Pass rush: B

Caleb Bacon’s switch from linebacker to defensive end seemed to pay off, finishing the day with a sack and a team-high three tackles for loss. However, the rest of the defensive line didn’t contribute much, as Penn State tallied just two sacks on the day.

Defensive backfield: A-

Through two drives, Penn State’s defense allowed just 14 yards, with six coming through the air. Zion Tracy and Josiah Zayas made several big plays on defense.

The Nittany Lions allowed just 103 passing yards on the day and tallied an interception late in the game off backup Zion Turner.

Linebackers: A-

After tearing his ACL last season, Rojas returned to Beaver Stadium as one of the best defenders of the day. With seven tackles, two tackles for loss and a sack, he was a primary key to the shutout.

Kooper Ebel — who was wearing the green dot — started off with several flashes and finished the day with three tackles and half a tackle for loss. Meanwhile, Cam Smith and Cael Brezina finished with four and five tackles, respectively.

Special teams: A

The only area Penn State’s special teams would be docked is Nathan Tiyce’s one touchback. However, the group had many good moments against Marshall, including 6-for-6 extra points and a 38-yard field goal from Ryan Barker, a downed punt at the 1-yard line and Robinson averaging 13.7 yards off his three punt returns.

title: ‘No surprise to us’ | Penn State DE Caleb Bacon makes name for himself at new position
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Defensive end Caleb Bacon joined Matt Campbell at Iowa State in 2021 as a walk-on before becoming a player who started every game with the Cyclones in 2025.

On Saturday, Bacon made a name for himself in his first game at Penn State and debuted as a defensive end, finishing second on the team with six tackles in the Nittany Lions’ win against Marshall.

“That might have been a little bit of a surprise to some fans,” linebacker Kooper Ebel said postgame. “Just seeing a new face out there, but man, that's no surprise to us. He's been doing that for a long time, and we're super happy.”

Bacon joined Penn State as a linebacker and worked at that spot through the spring and summer before testing out the waters as a defensive end to start fall camp. The move caught Bacon “off guard a little bit,” but his ability to “buy in” and trust the coaching staff has already paid dividends.

“The coaches I'm surrounded with, d-line coaches, really all of them have really bought into trying to make me a better player, and I really appreciate them for doing that,” Bacon said.

The quick adjustment came as no surprise to Campbell, who recognized Bacon’s work ethic following a season-ending injury in 2024. Bacon’s resilience to come back from that showed Campbell the type of player Bacon is and can become.

It came to fruition in Bacon’s first snaps as a defensive lineman, where in back-to-back plays he tackled Marshall quarterback Carlos Del Rio-Wilson behind the line of scrimmage.

“I think you guys got a chance to just see a little bit of just how special a player this guy is. He's tough. He's worked for everything he's got,” Campbell said.

Bacon had some experience playing up on the line of scrimmage at Iowa State, but that was in special schemes where he was moved to the edge. Now in D’Anton Lynn’s scheme, it’s the opposite, where he’s up on the line every play and will occasionally drop back into coverage.

The adjustment is something new to Bacon, but a change that he’s adapted to well. Ultimately, the play calling from Lynn “put us in great positions” for success against Marshall, leading to three tackles for loss for Bacon.

Bacon attributed his big game to his positional group. The change to defensive line came just over a month ago, and he’s already making a difference on the field, proving to be another chess piece for Lynn’s sometimes chaotic scheme.

“The d-lineman just took me in, been able to watch film with the guys in there, coaches, players, all of them, just learn what it takes to be a really good defensive lineman,” Bacon said.

title: Penn State cross country opens season sweeping Dolan Duals
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
While Penn State lost several of its top runners from last season due to graduation, it still performed at the top of its game in 2026.

The Nittany Lions opened the season against Lock Haven at the Dolan Duals on Friday, winning the men’s race 15-48 and the women’s race 15-50.

Here’s a look at how the blue and white took home the opening meet of the 2026 season.

Men’s 5,000m

Sophomore Isaac Opperman led the way for the men’s team after being one of the only true freshmen to compete last season. Against Lock Haven, he earned his first career victory, running 15:27.3.

Fellow sophomore Adam Kingston, who also saw action last year, finished a little over a second behind with a time of 15:28.7.

Brian DiCola was the first upperclassman to finish for either team, crossing the finish line in 15:33.8 for third place.

Freshman Thomas Rae finished fourth overall and was one of four freshmen to race for Penn State. He crossed the finish line in 15:34.3.

Woodland Hills, California, native Dorian Bening finished fifth for the Nittany Lions in a photo finish against Rae. He was another one of Penn State’s freshmen, finishing in 15:34.6.

Lock Haven junior Jakob Rager was the first athlete crossing the finish line for the Bald Eagles, finishing in sixth place. Less than half a second behind him was the third of the freshmen, Colin O’Donnell, who ran 15:35.2 for seventh place.

The Nittany Lions earned 15 of the top 18 spots in the race, including freshmen Justin Landis in 16th place.

Women’s 5,000m

Following a rising junior campaign, Claire Zubey earned her first cross country victory, running 17:29. She was followed by freshman Vivian Kipruto, who was five seconds behind in 17:34.

Sophomore Caroline Tribett competed in her first non-redshirted race on Friday, finishing third in 17:36.

A sizable gap followed Tribett, led by graduate Runner Katie Dallas. She continued Penn State’s sweep with a fourth-place finish, running 17:47.

The freshmen success continued as Gwynedd Valley, Pennsylvania, native Reese Miller finished less than a second behind in 17:50.

After an ankle injury limited her production during the second-half of the spring, graduate student Charlotte Costich finished sixth overall with a time of 17:57.

UNC Charlotte transfer Ella White rounded off the top-seven for the Nittany Lions as she crossed the finish line in 18:03 for her blue and white debut.

Anna Bondy was the last of the freshmen to race for Penn State, running 18:21 for 10th place.

The women’s squad took the first 12 places, with Lock Haven’s first runner coming in at 13th place.

Up next

The Nittany Lions will compete at the Harry Groves Spiked Shoe Invitational at Penn State, starting at 10 a.m. on Sept. 11.

title: ‘The sky’s the limit’ | Penn State WR Koby Howard’s breakout performance comes after offseason of hard work
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Koby Howard’s first catch of the 2026 season was a 42-yard touchdown reception. The sophomore found a wide-open gap in Marshall’s coverage and caught Rocco Becht’s pass at the 25-yard line before turning on the jets to outrun a pair of trailing defenders.

Howard had handed Penn State its first touchdown in the Matt Campbell era.

Those 42 yards were a fraction of his impact on the field. By the time he was taken off the field in the third quarter, he’d racked up 161 yards on six receptions, making him far and away the Nittany Lions’ top receiver to open the season.

“Going out there, being able to actually do it in the game, and not just in practice,” Howard said after the game. “A lot of people probably think of just doing it in practice, but being able to showcase it in the game really meant a lot to me.”

Arguably Howard’s defining play of the game was his last. Backup quarterback Alex Manske had recently checked in, and he let loose a lofting, 25-yard pass to Howard, who was under heavy pressure.

Howard jumped high in the air with his arms reaching over the defender’s head, snagging the ball and tumbling to the grass just inside the 15-yard line.

The Stripe Out crowd exploded in a chorus of cheers for a catch that set up Penn State’s fifth touchdown of the afternoon.

“I was like, ‘holy cow, no one's guarding him,’” Manske said. “I was trying to get a snap off. There ended up being a guy that ran out at the last second. I really didn't see him. When I put it in the air, I had a pretty good idea that Koby was going to come down with it. That was a crazy play, and that's the stuff Koby does.”

What made Howard truly effective was his ability to gain additional yardage after the reception. Of those 161 total receiving yards, 76 of them were earned after the catch by making swift cuts and burning the secondary with his speed.

Howard said this trait was “harped on a lot” at training camp by coach Kashif Moore.

For Howard’s teammates and coaches, the wide receiver’s performance was a result of the commitment and effort he displayed throughout the entire offseason.

Wide receiver Brett Eskildsen said that Howard’s breakout on Saturday was “only a matter of time.” Eskildsen put in a lot of effort getting to know Howard, and the pair trained with each other out in California and Florida.

“I've seen him work from the day I got here, and just being able to build that relationship together, I knew it was coming,” Eskildsen said after the game. “Whether it was today, next week, whenever it was coming, it was coming. It's unbelievable to see, it's well deserved and it didn't surprise any of us.”

Despite being promoted as one of the top receiving prospects last season, Howard barely saw the field under James Franklin but appeared in nine total games with 133 total receiving yards.

Howard surpassed that number in one game.

In an effort to take a step forward this year, Howard arrived at the training facility at 5:15 a.m. throughout the offseason to catch passes from the JUGS machine. Campbell has taken notice of that work ethic, and knew his opportunity would come soon enough.

However, Campbell also said that it’s important for Howard to remember that games like this one won’t happen every time. He noted that his ability to stay in the present will be huge for his development going forward.

“The sky’s the limit for Koby Howard,” Campbell said. “I’m really proud of him because it’s a great reward. Koby’s a guy that’s worked hard behind the scenes to take advantage of those moments. He’s got a chance to have a really special year for us.”

title: ‘That had nothing to do with me’ | Matt Campbell celebrates 1st Penn State victory crediting players, staff
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
As the team drove up Porter Road to Beaver Stadium, Matt Campbell wasn't the first person off the bus to greet the fans. He wasn't even the first coach off the bus.

Campbell’s Penn State debut featured the same humility he’s portrayed since he arrived in December. From the arrival off the bus to his postgame press conference, he continued to show that this isn’t about himself as a coach, but about the team and players he leads.

“You look up and you see those teams on our press box and some of the great coaches and players that played here, you’re just grateful to have the opportunity to lead a football team and continue to try to represent our fan base and the past of this program the right way,” Campbell said.

Campbell kept the focus off himself throughout his postgame press conference and on the field. He deferred a question asked about his personal emotions in Game 1 to talk about the assistant coaches and the team, and he de facto sprinted off the field so he could greet every player walking into the locker room.

His focus on the players was seen on the videoboard pregame as well. Campbell opted not to be announced alongside his starting lineup, saying with a laugh postgame “Yeah, I’m good on that. The scoreboard’s for the players.”

For some players, Campbell is the reason they’re at Penn State in the first place. Specifically, Alex Manske, who had his first action since open heart surgery, said that Campbell is why he transferred from Iowa State to the Nittany Lions.

“It means everything to me,” Manske said. “Following (Campbell) here, that was the goal the whole time because I knew what he could install in his program with the resources here.”

While playcalling was reserved for Taylor Mouser and D’Anton Lynn, Campbell’s focus was keeping the pace of the game and playing situational football.

Specifically, Campbell was tested with fourth downs today. He took a chance on a pair of fourth down conversions, electing to keep his offense on the field.

While the Nittany Lions converted both opportunities — resulting in touchdowns on both drives — Campbell took a risk on both chances.

“I’ll be honest with you, I didn’t know if that was a great call or not,” Campbell said with a laugh.

As Campbell walked away from Week 1 with a victory, marking the first Penn State coach with a shutout in their debut since 1915, he emphasized the importance of the families surrounding the program and pushed the credit away from himself.

“There’s a lot of young families that picked up and moved across the country because of their belief in what we were doing together,” Campbell said. “That had nothing to do with me. That was a we thing… (They’ve) really held a great standard in our program.”

title: ‘It felt great to be out there’ | Rocco Becht has efficient showing in Penn State debut
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Rocco Becht said Tuesday that “he might have a couple butterflies walking down the tunnel” prior to his first start in a Penn State uniform.

But Becht said postgame his stomach wasn’t fluttering as he expected. Instead, he was calm, and that coupled with his experience allowed him to have an efficient performance, going 13-for-18 with 271 yards and four touchdowns before being taken out in the third quarter in his Nittany Lions debut.

“I felt good. I honestly felt like I was gonna have a little more butterflies, and I was talking to some guys,” Becht said postgame. “It's probably because I'm a fifth-year dude, and so I'm a little older, so it felt normal to me. But it felt great to be out there.”

What Becht hadn’t experienced yet was a home entrance in Beaver Stadium, with his first coming in a Stripe Out environment with 108,489 fans behind him to begin the game.

“It was crazy to see everybody out there, the stripe fest that the fans were doing, and so to see the energy and feel the just environment and all was totally unique for me and different. So I was just excited to be a part of it,” Becht said.

Although the opening drive didn’t result in a touchdown, Becht showed his poise the next possession and got to experience his first Beaver Stadium crowd pop with a 42-yard throw to Koby Howard for his first touchdown pass at Penn State.

“Our running back fell getting out, which was probably where the ball was going to go,” Becht said. “ I had to move on. The o-line did a great job protecting me, and nobody was coming through. So we were able to do a kind of like an in-the-pocket scramble drill, and Koby did a good job of finding green grass.”

Becht’s first touchdown pass sparked the offensive momentum, leading to a dominant first half and proving there wasn’t any rust or kinks to be worked out despite the newness of the team.

The chemistry shown in the four-touchdown performance from the Nittany Lions’ quarterback was “a tribute to all the work and all the time he put into his craft” during the offseason, as wide receiver Brett Eskildsen put it.

Becht dished the ball to six different targets, finding both his wide receivers and tight ends during the game as the Nittany Lions raided Marshall through the air.

“I think for Rocco to be able to handle that and distribute the ball, sometimes being a great quarterback is like being a great point guard, right?” Campbell said. “You got to be a great distributor of where the ball needs to go, and I thought he was outstanding today.”

Becht’s final touchdown pass of the day came on Penn State’s first drive of the second half with a bullet to his former Iowa State teammate Zay Robinson capping off his first showing in Beaver Stadium.

The touchdown pass in the third quarter gave Penn State a 31-0 lead, and allowed Becht to fully take in his first experience with a full crowd at Beaver Stadium, allowing his backup Alex Manske to get some playing time.

“I think when I got pulled in the third quarter when my day was over, I think just taking it all in at that moment, knowing that I played my first game at Beaver Stadium,” Becht said. “The way that we did it, we did it at a smooth rate, a clean rate, no turnovers… I think everything just coming together as one, us going out there playing as one team was great.”

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State's shutout win over Marshall
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State began the Matt Campbell era in front of a Stripe Out crowd against Marshall Saturday.

The Nittany Lions gave the Happy Valley faithful plenty to cheer for as Penn State routed the Thundering Herd, 45-0, behind an emerging pass rusher and a huge game from Koby Howard.

Here’s three takeaways from Penn State’s opening game win.

Caleb Bacon's move to DE paid off

Caleb Bacon initially made the switch to edge rusher to begin fall camp as Campbell felt the team would be “missing the boat not to start him off in fall camp on the edge.”

Bacon’s move to defensive end became official on Aug. 30, and Saturday showed why he made the change.

The redshirt senior was the beneficiary of multiple unique schemes, featuring additional edge rushers throughout the defensive line. Bacon’s power, mixed with speed from the edge, proved to be a difference maker on multiple drives in the first half.

Bacon totaled six tackles, three tackles for loss and a sack, moving around the defense line in the opening half.

Penn State proved it could get to the quarterback, sacking Marshall quarterback Carlos Del Rio-Wilson twice, while also stopping any running opportunities for the dual-threat quarterback. With Bacon’s performance, the pass rush adds even more depth and could be a big part to the Nittany Lions’ defensive production.

Wide receiver outburst

Campbell said at local media day that Penn State would likely be in 12 or 13 personnel on most occasions on offense. However, in the team’s first game, it was the wide receivers who created separation and connected with Rocco Becht.

The receivers were Becht’s go-to targets despite the hype surrounding the tight ends during the offseason. Howard, Brett Eskildsen and Chase Sowell all made key catches and big plays to get Penn State out to a big lead in the first quarter.

It was Howard, however, who emerged as Becht’s top target in the first half.

Howard’s first reception of the season went for a 42-yard touchdown after Becht found him wide open in the middle of the field. Howard totaled 81 yards in the first quarter and 123 in the first half.

The sophomore proved he can do it all with another catch in the middle of the field before making people miss. He capped off his game with a catch over top of a defender, ending with 161 yards, more than he had in all of 2025.

Eskildsen and Zay Robinson also got in on the receiving parade, both catching touchdown passes from Becht.

The tight ends totaled just two catches, in comparison to 14 from the wide receivers, before Campbell deployed the backups in a blowout. Benjamin Brahmer did get on the board with a touchdown, though.

Running backs struggle

The biggest position group to be affected by the outburst from the receivers was the running backs, and when they got their chance to move the ball, they didn’t produce.

Carson Hansen and James Peoples were the two backs to get action in the first half, but neither was consistent.

The duo combined for 18 rushes and 73 yards, totaling just over four yards per carry. On one drive, Peoples was given three straight carries and couldn’t get the first down, gaining nine yards.

It wasn’t until Quinton Martin Jr. came into the game in the second half that Penn State showed signs of consistently running the ball well. Martin and Cam Wallace each ran in a 6-yard rushing touchdown, but none of the running backs could put together consistency.

While the running game’s struggles didn’t make a difference in the final score, if it continues this way, it could come back to hurt the Nittany Lions later in the season.

title: Penn State names captains for Week 1 against Marshall
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State's captains have been named for Week 1.

Offensive lineman Anthony Donkoh, quarterback Rocco Becht, linebacker Kooper Ebel and long snapper Blaise Sokach-Minnick were announced to be the captains for the season-opener against Marshall.

Becht and Ebel have prior experience as captains on a game-by-game basis at Iowa State, while Donkoh and Sokach-Minnick are debuting their "C."

Last year, Penn State's captains were named for the full season. However, Matt Campbell brought his game-by-game policy to Happy Valley.

"That might be a thing where we put finality to that probably, maybe even a little bit later in the season," Campbell said Wednesday. "It's a unique time in this team, and I think there's a lot of guys that certainly you know maybe deserve the right to be that, especially when you saw the vote from our football team. So I think we'll just kind of navigate that probably one game at a time as we get into it."

The Nittany Lions will face Marshall on Saturday at Beaver Stadium at 3:30 p.m.

title: Clean sheet supported by controlled attack leads Penn State men's soccer to win over Yale
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
Following back-to-back losses to Missouri State and Pitt, the Nittany Lions return to the win column following a 1-0 victory against Yale at Jeffrey Field on Friday night. The blue and white played a complete game, controlling the match on both sides of the ball.

The Penn State defense recorded its first clean sheet of the season, allowing no shots on goal through all 90 minutes of play. The box score doesn’t tell the entire story for the offense, which held possession for the majority of the match.

The key to the Nittany Lions’ ball control was patience. Yale dropped eight players back while having two attackers pressure the ball up top. The backline of the blue and white passed back-and-forth, retaining the ball until it could find a midfielder with enough space to advance forward.

“We needed to control the tempo of the game with the ball, and the only way to do that was to get our wing backs really high and to get more numbers than their half,” coach Rob Dow said. “We have three versus their two in the back, and always have that option to swing it back and forth.”

For the initial 15 minutes, the match was a stalemate with both defenses holding their own. The Bulldogs weren’t allowing passes sent to runs downfield, and Penn State collected opposing passes downfield through the air.

After a couple offensive pushes by the blue and white, it began to find the formula. When the midfield could find space, Penn State was able to get the ball to the wing, who sent multiple crosses in for goal scoring opportunities.

While that attacking scheme was a group effort, freshman forward Nehan Hasan added a sense of flair and speed that couldn’t go unnoticed. On multiple occasions, Hasan used his footwork and skill moves to create chances for himself and his teammates.

“Every time he touched the ball, he caused some problems for the defense,” Dow said. “For a young player like him, the courage he’s showing, I’m proud of him.”

In the opening minutes of the second half, Hasan’s technical dribbling led to an assist on the right side, which sophomore defender Joe Buckley finished with a first-time shot into the back of the net. The two linked up for the first points of each of their collegiate careers.

“I just try to drive at pace and then see what’s around me,” Hasan said. “If it’s time to take them on, I try to do a little move, if not, I try to recycle it and play with my teammates.”

Buckley’s goal accelerated Penn State’s momentum, which they carried through their second win of the season.

Penn State will look to build off their performance when it travels to the West Coast to face defending national champion and 11th-ranked Washington next Friday.

title: Penn State men's soccer shuts down Yale, gets back in win column
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State was looking to get back into the win column after losing its last two matches. The blue and white faced off against its last opponent before entering conference play on a partly-cloudy Friday and THON night. Ultimately the Nittany Lions would beat Yale 1-0 in a dominant offensive performance.

1st Half

The game started off with a couple high-flying balls with Yale then getting a quick crosser off but the shot was not there. Penn State replied with a throw-in towards the Bulldogs box but a foul would kill the momentum.

Both teams struggled to find any offensive rhythm through the first ten minutes of play, often turning the ball over when entering the middle of enemy territory. The blue and white made the first real goal attempt of the game around the 12th minute with a fast break sprint that ultimately met the hands of Bulldog goalkeeper Josh Linebaugh.

The Nittany Lions were the first to add subs in the 20th minute after lots of back and forth towards the middle of the pitch. Through the first portion of the first half Penn State dominated offensive possession, looking like the clear better team, but the match remained scoreless.

The first corner kick of the game came in the 26th minute, but only resulted in a couple Yale throw-ins. Penn State continued to dominate offensive possession through the first half but the Bulldog defenders seemed to be playing in a bend-not-break style. A highlight for the blue and white was the ball movement upfield.

In the 33rd minute Nittany Lion defensemen Nehan Hasan broke two defenders' ankles in the box but came up short with his shot being blocked.

“I thought he drew into the game really well, he looked good every time he touched the ball,” coach Rob Dow said about Hasan’s performance.

Yale’s first play in Penn State territory in a while came during the 37th minute from a free kick which turned into a corner for the Bulldogs, but they would come up empty, keeping the game scoreless.

The Nittany Lions last chance to score in the first half came in the 41st minute but Yale’s defenders stonewalled them yet again. The blue and white completely dominated possession the entire 1st half of play and Yale seemed to be playing with a defensive identity, having six guys in the back line.

2nd Half

As a beautiful sunset fell on Jeffrey Field both teams prepared for the second half of action in this matchup.

Penn State continued its offensive takeover with a couple of shots to start the period. A goal kick from keeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese started a play that ended when defensemen Joe Buckley softly put a shot in the bottom right of the net for the first score of the game, assisted by Hasan, giving the Nittany Lions a 1-0 lead in the 49th minute of play.

“It definitely felt good,” Hasan said, talking about his assist after the game. “Buckley did a great job being in a spot, Toby played a great ball and I just had to cut it back.”

The blue and white continued its offensive onslaught shortly after with a couple of great shot attempts that led to two corner kicks. Bulldog midfielder Nathan Harmon picked up the first card of the game with a yellow in the 57th minute. Penn State defensemen Beckham Brown came off the field holding his head after the play.

Yale made many attempts to make a goal of their own, but found themselves turning the ball over and committing fouls, which limited their opportunities. Penn State wasn’t as dominant offensively in the second half, spending more time in their own territory than it did the entire first half.

The blue and white had a major play in motion when Yale defensemen Danny Grumann committed a foul for the second yellow of the game, however the free kick resulted in nothing.

Yale had its first shot on goal in the 82nd minute from forward Simon Adjakple, who then went down. That opportunity was followed by another great shot attempt from Bulldog forward Sebi Roy in the 85th.

Penn State’s defense would hold strong the rest of the match, but Dow had some different thoughts postgame.

“We gave them opportunities late in the game,” Dow said. “We need to see out games on the ball, especially when we win the ball, making sound decisions so that's on us.”

Up Next

The Nittany Lions travel across the coast to face the Washington Huskies in Seattle at 10:30 p.m. next Friday.

“They are gonna be better than any other game that we’ve played so far, but we're focused on Washington,” Dow said.

title: Penn State field hockey beats Villanova 2-0 in a battle of two opposite halves
author: Owen Lomotan I The Daily Collegian
description:
After splitting their first two home games this past weekend, the Nittany Lions looked to continue their dominance against Villanova. Penn State was coming off an 8-0 blowout win over Lock Haven, a game in which seven different players scored goals for the blue and white.

After a quiet first half, the Nittany Lions came out of halftime with a more aggressive approach, ultimately producing the only two goals of the afternoon.

The shift was especially noticeable on penalty corners, where Penn State turned increased pressure into scoring opportunities. The ability to recognize what was not working early and adjust on the fly became one of the biggest differences between the two sides.

Against the Wildcats, the Nittany Lions were locked in a tight battle from the beginning, dominated by foul calls. Neither team scored in a first half that only saw one penalty corner for Penn State, taken by junior forward Ella Gaitan with 1:39 remaining in the second quarter.

The blue and white were held to only five shots in the first half, three of which were taken by senior midfielder Natalie Freeman.

The Nittany Lions held Villanova to only four shots in the first half and gave up no penalty corners in the process.

The second half was much different. Penn State began attacking with greater urgency, putting more pressure on Villanova's defense, and allowing for more penalty corner opportunities.

This adjustment gave Penn State something it had been missing early: sustained pressure in dangerous areas of the field. Instead of allowing the game to remain a defensive battle, the Nittany Lions began forcing Villanova to respond to them.

The third quarter saw Penn State play a much more aggressive style that rewarded them with two more penalty corners, one of which resulted in the first goal for the Nittany Lions, scored by Freeman.

The goal was significant beyond simply putting Penn State ahead. After struggling to generate much offensive momentum in the first half, the Nittany Lions had finally turned one of their second-half opportunities into a result.

Sophomore defender Cooper Cutchins came up with a crucial block on the Wildcat penalty corner with under a minute to play in the third to keep the narrow lead for the Nittany Lions.

The fourth quarter saw a rise in urgency for the blue and white. The Nittany Lion defense stopped back-to-back Villanova penalty corners, and converted off one of their own from a strike by Purdy.

While Penn State's second-half adjustment was most obvious on the attacking end, the same mentality carried over to its defense. Villanova's penalty corners represented some of the Wildcats' best opportunities to erase the deficit, but Penn State's defense responded when the pressure increased.

The difference between the two halves wasn’t lost on the Nittany Lions. For Penn State, the game became less about what happened during the opening 30 minutes and more about how the team responded to what it saw.

“I think as a team we just talked a lot about starting strong and ending strong”, Freeman said. “Over the past season, that’s been a focus point for us, is scoring in [the] first half. For us to finally notch it in the second [half], that’s a big momentum shift. That’s when the gates sort of opened for us as a team”.

Penn State’s ability to make key adjustments at halftime has been a huge reason for their success as of late.

“Getting to halftime and having that talk as a team and figuring out what our weak links are at that moment”, Freeman said. “We talked a lot about the press and organizing, adjusting that on the fly and adapting and recognizing what was going on so that we’re not letting nearly as many balls come through the center. That was really big for us. Somebody makes a big stop, it’s contagious”.

Additionally, junior goalkeeper Aby Deverka posted her second straight shutout game.

“It’s just super exciting to have two in a row, and I think just rolling into the next one, having that confidence that this is something that we did as a team together”, Deverka said. “We can do it again if we consistently show up every day”.

The Nittany Lions have now played two games in a row where they haven’t scored in the opening quarter, yet were able to make a second half push that won them the edge over their opponents. Coach Hannah Prince has never failed to see her team make the big plays when they matter most.

For Prince, the halftime conversation was less about panicking over a scoreless opening half and more about identifying exactly where Penn State needed to improve.

“I think it says a lot. A lot about their grit and just intensity that they know is within them,” Prince said. “But at the same time, I think it’s really important for us to continue to reflect on how we can have a stronger start in the first half so we’re not just relying on the second half.”

The win offered Penn State more than another mark in the win column. It provided another example of a team capable of changing its approach when its initial plan isn’t producing the desired results.

While Prince emphasized the need for stronger starts, Penn State has already demonstrated that it can recognize problems, make adjustments and find another level when the game demands it.

The Nittany Lions now prepare to welcome Delaware at noon Sunday.

title: Penn State field hockey defeats Villanova for second straight shutout victory
author: Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian
description:
Coming off of a monstrous 8-0 victory over Lock Haven for the first of Hannah Prince’s tenure in Happy Valley, Penn State continued its home stretch, welcoming Villanova on Friday afternoon.

The Nittany Lions entered the matchup with plenty of momentum, looking to build on their impressive offensive performance from the previous weekend while maintaining the defensive consistency that had helped them find success early in the season.

Momentum stuck for the blue and white, posting its second straight shutout win by defeating the Wildcats 2-0 thanks to a strong second half.

Penn State senior midfielder/forward Natalie Freeman was all over the field, contributing to both of the Nittany Lions’ points, including a third-period goal to get the blue and white on the board.

The game was as tight as could be between two teams looking to continue their winning ways, both coming off blowout wins last Sunday. From the opening drop to the final whistle in the fourth period, it was a defensive masterclass from the Nittany Lions.

Goalie Aby Deverka kept the Wildcats out of the net with four saves, leaving more opportunity for the Nittany Lions to push the ball up the field, and it paid dividends. Despite this, it still took the blue and white’s offense an entire half to get going and open up the game.

The second period served as a precursor to what was to follow, as the Nittany Lions looked more than prepared to score, with three of their 13 shots coming in this frame. Freeman’s poise to score showed both here and in the third period.

The last 30 minutes of game time were when the Nittany Lions shined the most, both offensively and defensively.

Sophomore midfielder/forward, Joji Purdy, also contributed to the scoring of the Nittany Lions, netting one through off a pass from Lara Pyle and a Freeman corner that set it all up in the fourth period.

Penn State served up nine shots, put through two goals, and three of Deverka’s four saves came all within the dominant second half. This helped the blue and white claw out a hard-fought win in Happy Valley for its second straight win.

Despite the shutout win, one thing that may come up in preparation for the rest of the season for the Nittany Lions is that of discipline. Sophomore midfielder Cooper Cutchins earned an uncalled for yellow card in the final two minutes of a game that was essentially at its end.

Villanova will follow up this loss with a return to Snell Field, playing a visiting New Haven team in what should serve as a get-back game for the Wildcats.

Up Next

Penn State will ride its two-game winning streak into an early Sunday matchup, playing host to the Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens. The Blue Hens are coming off a 2-1 win against then-No.18 Monmouth and will enter University Park in the second leg of their four-game road trip.

On the flip side, the upcoming matchup will mark the fourth game of the blue and white’s six-game home stretch.

title: ‘He’s finally getting honored’ | Penn State alumni, fans share thoughts on Paterno Family Experience Room
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Sharyn Fitzpatrick-Skudneski, 69, and Judy Hoffman, 55, beamed from ear to ear as they entered the Paterno Family Experience Room on Friday morning. Two of the three superfans dubbed the “PSU Crazies” couldn’t help but reminisce on the past.

Fitzpatrick-Skudneski was immediately struck by the featured exhibit — an authentic replica of the late coach Joe Paterno’s office. It was complete with the exact furniture he used during his tenure including the Greenberg Chair, film machine, playbook notes and a box of Wheaties with his face on it from 2003.

“He’s finally getting honored,” Fitzpatrick-Skudneski said. “This touches the surface very little of who (Joe) was and what he's done.”

The Paterno Family Experience Room opened on Thursday inside the All-Sports Museum at Beaver Stadium and consists of Paterno’s office, a timeline of his career, an evolutionary display of helmets, a list of the team’s captains, Hall of Fame inductees — both collegiate and professional — and interactive video boards.

Fitzpatrick-Skudneski, decked out in Penn State merchandise from head to toe, looked at a picture of Paterno and immediately thought about the Paterno family’s influence on her life.

She was serving as the Treasurer for the Penn State Alumni Association Chapter in San Francisco. She attended a Paterno alumni banquet in Palo Alto, California, and Paterno himself introduced her to the president of the Silicon Valley Chapter, Stan Skudneski, who she later married in 1993.

“I was talking to Sue (Paterno). I had seen her at the natatorium a lot swimming, and my husband knew Joe. So, Joe comes over saying, ‘You kids need to meet each other,’ and he introduced us,” Fitzpatrick-Skudneski said. “(Stan’s) treasurer didn't show up for the night, so I had to write a check for 650 people for dinner, and he met me the next day at the bank.”

Fitzpatrick-Skudneski and Hoffman read the timeline of Paterno’s life, looked at the wall of trophies and laughed while remembering the hundreds of experiences they’ve shared throughout the years.

On the other end of the floor, John Powers, 47, and his family came to State College from Tampa Bay, Florida, for the season-opener against Marshall on Saturday and decided to stop by the Penn State All-Sports Museum a day ahead of the game.

Powers couldn’t keep his eyes off the wall featuring all of the team’s captains since 1887. Powers said that it’s important to include such an exhibit to give his children the chance to learn the program’s history.

“The best part is bringing my kids here and letting them experience it,” Powers said. “Obviously, it’s biased towards getting them to become Nittany Lions someday, but just having them relive it and see this for themselves is great.”

Bruce Engle, 75, was also lost in a sea of memories. A 1973 graduate, Engle was the Scholarship Chair of the Penn State Alumni Association’s South Jersey Shore Chapter, and he vividly remembered meeting the Paterno family on many occasions, even having dinner with them in Philadelphia.

“It brings back very great memories to be able to see everything put in this fashion, just to see it and reminisce on all the pictures,” Engle said.

Engle smiled as he gazed at Paterno’s replica office. He’s been a season ticket holder since 1974 and experienced first-hand the changes that have been made since his days as a student.

However, Engle said that it’s “marvelous and unique” that the Paterno Family Experience Room was able to preserve a slice of history as it stood.

“This is a marvelous testament to a great coach, and a great family man, and everything that he stood for,” Engle said. “It's been a long time coming, and it's a marvelous job they did with this.”

title: Penn State to honor Dr. Wayne J. Sebastianelli against Marshall
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State announced Friday that it'll honor the life and legacy of Dr. Wayne J. Sebastianelli with a helmet sticker and moment of silence on Saturday against Marshall.

Sebastianelli served as Penn State's director of athletic medicine for 30 years and died on May 5, as announced by Penn State Athletics.

The sticker will be on the back left of the helmet, with a black background and Sebastianelli's initials, "WSJ," written in white.

Sebastianelli was notably the doctor who first treated Penn State cornerback Adam Taliaferro on the field, keeping him from paralysis during recovery, while also treating many other Penn State athletes during his 38-year career with athletics.

Sebastianelli was also a member of the Big Ten Sports Medicine committee while serving as the chief of staff at Mount Nittany Surgical Center for 16 years, becoming a staple of medicine in the Penn State community.

title: Sandusky evidentiary hearing to proceed as scheduled; he will appear remotely
author: Kahlie Wray | Editor-in-Chief
description:
Jerry Sandusky evidentiary hearing will proceed as scheduled on Tuesday at 9:30 a.m.

His attorney filed a request on Friday to have the hearing canceled, as he is planning to seek federal habeas relief — a legal procedure where individuals can challenge their detention — according to reporting from ESPN.

His request was denied at a status conference on Friday.

Sandusky, 82, was convicted in 2012 of 45 counts of child sexual abuse young boys. He was originally sentenced to 30 to 60 years in prison.

He will appear remotely.

One of the men who alleged the former Penn State assistant coach assaulted him when he was young, is expected to recant his testimony.

title: Players to watch | QB Carlos Del Rio-Wilson highlights Marshall’s roster
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State will begin the Matt Campbell era and open up its season with a favorable matchup against a Marshall team in the Sun Belt that went 5-7 a year ago.

The Thundering Herd are no strangers to traveling to a ranked Power Four team to start the season, as it took on then-No. 5 Georgia to open 2025.

Marshall brought in a large number of transfers this offseason — similar to Penn State — in Tony Gibson’s second year as the head coach of the program.

A majority of the returning starters are experienced players, which could prove to be a more difficult matchup than most think for a brand new Penn State team.

Here’s a few veteran players to watch who could have big days on Saturday.

Carlos Del Rio-Wilson, quarterback

Marshall’s team revolves around the quarterback, Carlos Del Rio-Wilson, who returns for his second year at Marshall. Del Rio-Wilson transferred from Syracuse after the 2024 season and started for the Thundering Herd in 2025.

Del Rio-Wilson is the Preseason Sun Belt Offensive Player of the Year, and his dual threat capabilities could cause issues for a Penn State defense that’s yet to play together against a real opponent.

The quarterback rushed for 661 yards and six touchdowns last year, while tossing 2,043 yards and 17 touchdowns through the air. Dual-threat quarterbacks gave the Nittany Lions fits a season ago, but with a new coordinator and fresh faces on the defense, the unit’s ability to shut down a quarterback with Del Rio-Wilson’s versatility is unknown.

Del Rio-Wilson is one of two quarterbacks returning in 2026 to have thrown for 2,000 yards, rushed for 600 yards and completed 65% of his passes last season.

Demarcus Lacey, wide receiver

Del Rio-Wilson’s favorite target from a season ago was Demarcus Lacey, who returned to Marshall for his redshirt senior season in 2026.

Lacey doesn’t bring any daunting size, standing at just 6-foot, but his connection with Del Rio-Wilson could play a major factor. The size will be favorable for Penn State’s likely top cornerback Audavion Collins, who stands at 5-foot-11.

The receiver played in all 12 games for the Thundering Herd last year, catching 65 passes for 769 yards and five touchdowns. An 11.8 yards per reception mark shows Lacey’s ability to make big plays, something that could be key to a potential upset of the Nittany Lions.

Lacey will be Del Rio-Wilson’s top target again in 2026, and when the team throws the ball, he’s likely the first look for the redshirt senior connection.

Javae Gilmore, linebacker

Javae Gilmore brings size to the linebacker room for Marshall. The 6-foot-4 linebacker is one of the team’s returning leaders in tackles from a season ago.

Gilmore was a standout at the line of scrimmage, totaling 11.5 tackles for loss last year. That talent to snuff the run could prevent Penn State’s rushing attack from gaining momentum.

The linebacker had two tackles against Georgia in 2025, but had a season-best 13 tackles against Penn State center Brock Riker’s former team Texas State on Oct. 18.

Gilmore is another experienced player on Marshall’s roster, and that veteran presence could get the Thundering Herd out to a quick start on Saturday.

Boogie Trotter, cornerback

Boogie Trotter’s status for Saturday’s matchup is now back on. Trotter was removed from Marshall’s roster Wednesday after a preliminary injunction denied Trotter’s eligibility opportunity for 2026.

However, Trotter was re-added to the Thundering Herd’s roster on Thursday, giving him a chance to play on Saturday.

Trotter’s presence would be huge for Marshall, as he totaled 74 tackles and five interceptions last season. Two of those picks were returned for touchdowns.

The redshirt senior could be a pest to Rocco Becht’s rhythm if he plays Saturday, likely matching up with the Nittany Lions’ top receiver on any given play.

title: Mackenzie Gress' career night keeps Penn State women's soccer alive in draw with Virginia Tech
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Netminder Mackenzie Gress helped keep Penn State alive in its draw against Virginia Tech at Jeffrey Field on Thursday night . The redshirt senior goalkeeper made several key saves for Nittany Lions in the contest, ending the game with 10 saves, the most in a single match in her career.

This standout performance gave Penn State a chance to hold their lead throughout the match, even as Virginia Tech created pressure for most of the second half.

Gress entered the matchup already playing some of the best soccer of her career as the blue and white’s previous two victories were shutouts against Bucknell and Brown. These performances led the Penn State veteran netminder to be named Big Ten Goalkeeper of the week.

The shot-stopper has been Penn State's starting goalkeeper for the last three seasons steadily getting better every single year but in 2026 Gress has made the biggest jump of her career collecting 21 saves in five matches, already a quarter away from her 60 save total in 2025.

Gress was tested early with Virginia Tech handling most of the possession. The Lyndhurst, New Jersey, native, made the first of her many saves in the second minute that allowed Penn State to hold momentum and keep possession for the rest of the first half.

The redshirt senior held her own in the second half with clutch saves against Virginia Tech's Anna Garrow and Eliana Salama that were particularly important late in the game as the Hokies were taking control of the match.

Despite Gress’ impressive performance the Hokies broke the seal in the 85th minute when Gabby Ciocca's shot just got past Gress to make the score 1-1. This ultimately ended the match in a draw, but despite the result Gress was one of the biggest reasons Penn State remained in position to win deep into the second half.

The Nittany Lions came out flat in the second half, similar to their lone loss on the season against West Virginia, but Gress was able to be the anchor of the defense and keep the blue and white steady. Her presence in net was the driving force in the second half for the Nittany Lions and helped the blue and white avoid the loss column.

This result moved Penn State to 2-1-2 on the season while Virginia Tech moved to 4-0-3. For the Nittany Lions, the late equalizer will likely leave the team wanting more after a game where the backline played well, but for Gress, the performance further reinforced her importance between the posts for the Nittany Lions program.

The redshirt senior entered the season having started all 21 matches for Penn State in 2025, recording 60 saves, three shutouts and a .706 save-percentage.

Against the Hokies, the experienced goalkeeper once again showed why Penn State trusts her between the posts and also solidified her potential to be one of the best netminders in the Big Ten. The Nittany Lions couldn’t hold onto their lead, but Gress gave them every opportunity to do so, and for most of Thursday night that was enough.

title: ‘Anyone can enjoy art’ | Palmer Museum of Art serves students, community alike
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Palmer Museum of Art on University Park campus houses the largest collection of art between Pittsburgh and Philadelphia.

Palmer, located on 650 Bigler Rd., is a free-admission art museum that serves both Penn State and Central Pennsylvania alike. It offers a plethora of programs and tours, and frequently features new art exhibitions. It’s open Wednesday through Saturday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Thursday’s hours are extended to 8 p.m., and Sunday's hours are from noon to 5 p.m.

Director Amanda Hellman has only been in her position at the museum for eight months, but she said she constantly strives to create a welcoming space.

“Every day feels very different,” Hellman said. “I spend a lot of time meeting with everybody, setting a vision for the institution and helping people establish workflows and how we accomplish that.”

Since assuming her position at the Palmer, Hellman has set forth big goals for the museum by creating an exhibition program for the next five years, working toward accreditation with the American Alliance of Museums and ensuring the new building is meeting the community's needs.

“This (accreditation) is important because it allows us to get bigger grants and to partner with other credited institutions, because they know that we’re following best practices,” Hellman said.

Along with that initiative, another important part of the museum's philosophy is Penn State’s land-grant mission, which is a three-fold commitment to teaching, research and public service aimed at benefiting all residents of the Commonwealth.

For Janine Yorimoto Boldt, Palmer Museum’s curator of American art, it's a vital part of her job. As a curator, Boldt thinks carefully about how to make those connections between the university, students, faculty and researchers as they study and interpret American art.

It’s important, Boldt said, to take into consideration the origins of the land-grant, as the land-grant mission relied on the sale of lands that are native lands and the dispossession of indigenous communities to fund the university.

“I have a long-term goal of a project that will think through the entangled histories of land-grant universities and indigenous dispossession through the visual arts,” Boldt said.

Recently, Boldt has purchased two photographs by native photographers Tom Jones and Ryan RedCorn, who represent contemporary native individuals. She said she wanted to grow their collection to include positive representations of native people by native artists.

On Oct. 8 at 5:30 p.m., RedCorn will deliver a speech and install his own photograph. He will also meet with the Indigenous Peoples' Student Association and the Indigenous Faculty and Staff Alliance at Penn State.

Boldt’s largest project, currently, is planning for a complete reinstallation of the American art galleries on the museum’s first floor.

“I’m spending a lot of time browsing our collection, doing research, thinking about how to reorganize and reinterpret that collection,” Boldt said.

As the museum approaches the reinstallation, Boldt said she is thinking of key themes for each of the galleries, and how they can remain flexible to allow for a regular rotation of artworks.

“(Boldt) really sought faculty, student and community member input on reimagining the American galleries, which is the strength of the museum’s collection,” Keri Mongelluzzo, the museum’s educator for academic engagement and access, said.

For students looking to get involved, the Palmer offers numerous opportunities; there’s something for everyone. Students can become ambassadors and interns, or they can merely attend events like “Art After Hours.”

Mongelluzzo oversees the undergraduate internship program at the Palmer to manage and provide leadership for the students. She said it’s open to students from all colleges to work in various museum departments.

She also organizes class visits for all colleges on campus, working with faculty to align the museum's collections to what they’re teaching. She said they teach through art to help students develop the core skills and concepts relevant to their disciplines.

Last year, Palmer had roughly 200 curricular engagements with classes. This fall, it’ll host around four to six class visits every Thursday.

Amanda Demuth, a fourth-year studying art history and philosophy, has been a student intern at the museum for three years. She’s worked with Mongelluzzo on public programming, and this year, she’s assisting Boldt with research.

“You don’t have to know anything about history, anything about art in order to intern or volunteer for the museum because there are people there that want to help you,” Demuth said.

As an undergraduate student, Demuth said her internship with the Palmer has helped her gain knowledge and perspective that she otherwise wouldn’t have experienced in a classroom setting. She said Mongelluzzo has shown her that professionalism doesn’t always have to be cut and dry.

“It’s just a good way to get involved, not just with a student community, but also with the State College community,” Demuth said.

Her favorite aspect of the museum, she said, is being able to reach communities that wouldn’t normally feel like they’re welcome in museums.

“Anyone can enjoy art, anyone can go to a museum and love it,” Demuth said. “You don’t have to understand everything.”

Anyone who’s interested in visiting the Palmer soon can look forward to the first “Art After Hours” event, which will take place Sept. 24 from 5 to 8 p.m. This event allows students to create their own art, as well as hear from Penn State student artists featured in the museum’s current exhibition titled “Dreaming American Futures: Invitational 250.”

“Come spend your time here, study here, look at stuff, challenge yourself, bring friends,” Mongelluzzo said.

title: Penn State vs. Marshall preview | Weather, injury updates and more
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Matt Campbell era is finally here.

Penn State will open the 2026 season on Saturday, facing Marshall at 3:30 p.m. in Beaver Stadium.

The Nittany Lions have won the last six straight season openers and will be looking to do so again this weekend.

Here’s a look at what to expect Week 1, from weather to betting odds and more.

Forecast

After a week of rain and thunderstorms, Saturday’s forecast will be great for the first game of 2026.

According to AccuWeather, there’ll be a high of 77 degrees, with a real feel of 80 degrees, on Saturday. As the evening rolls around, it will move to a high of 54 degrees and a real feel of 56 degrees.

There’s only a 20% chance of precipitation on Saturday, and it’s expected to be less humid than earlier in the week.

Betting, how to watch

The Nittany Lions are the heavy favorites over Marshall.

Penn State is a 24.5-point favorite over the Thundering Herd, according to FanDuel. The over/under is set at 52.5 points. These odds mean Penn State is expected to have a 38-14 victory.

The matchup will be broadcast on Fox Sports 1, while tickets are available on Ticketmaster for as low as $10.

About Marshall

The Thundering Herd are coming off a 2025 campaign where they went 5-7, including a 45-7 loss against their only Power Four opponent, Georgia.

However, Marshall returns several players this year who are slated for improved seasons, including quarterback Carlos Del Rio-Wilson.

Del Rio-Wilson served as a dual-threat quarterback last year, throwing for 2,043 and rushing for 749 yards — both team highs. The redshirt senior has some high expectations, as he was named to the Davey O’Brien Award watch list in August, an honor given annually to the top quarterback in the country.

Outside of Del Rio-Wilson, Marshall has few other options in the run game. It has just four running backs on its roster, with only one averaging multiple carries per game last season.

Marshall’s leading receiver Demarcus Lacey and top defender Boogie Trotter have faced eligibility lawsuits throughout the offseason, but are on the official roster as of Thursday afternoon. It’s unclear whether they’ll be available on Saturday.

Returning tight end Toby Payne recorded the next-highest receiving yards last year with 393 yards and three touchdowns.

Two of the defenders Penn State will need to keep an eye on are linebacker Javae Gilmore and defensive lineman Braydin Ward. Gilmore recorded 63 tackles and 11.5 tackles for loss last season, while Ward had five tackles and four forced fumbles.

About Penn State

Penn State enters the 2026 season as one of the more uncertain teams in the country, as it has 62 new faces this season, including 24 players from Iowa State.

Among the new faces are Rocco Becht, who came to Penn State as the winningest returning quarterback in college football. Becht had a down year by his standards in 2025, but he was also dealing with a torn labrum in his left shoulder and an AC joint sprain in his right.

Now healthy, Becht is in his best form yet, according to Campbell.

Taylor Mouser said Tuesday that the Nittany Lions have many weapons on offense that could be played throughout the game.

For the running backs, that includes Carson Hansen, James Peoples, Quinton Martin Jr. and Cam Wallace. Each of the four are expected to share time in the backfield and bring varied experience to the running back room.

Becht will have several options in the passing game as well, including seven wide receivers Mouser named as players he has trust in: Chase Sowell, Amarion Jackson, Koby Howard, Zay Robinson, Brett Eskildsen, Keith Jones Jr. and Karon Brookins.

Penn State’s tight end room, however, boasts some of the best players on the team. Campbell said at local media day to expect multiple tight ends to be on the field at a time, with the three main guys being Benjamin Brahmer, Andrew Rappleyea and Gabe Burkle.

Defensively, several players are expected to play big roles for the Nittany Lions.

Linebacker Tony Rojas and cornerbacks Zion Tracy and Audavion Collins are among the more experienced returners on Penn State’s roster. However, transfers Kooper Ebel, Jeremiah Cooper and Marcus Neal Jr. also bring a fair share of experience to the defense.

Injury updates

Cooper, Burkle and linebacker Alex Tatsch are still recovering from long-term injuries, but all three are back practicing with the team.

Campbell said Tuesday that Cooper is the closest to returning, giving his star safety a “probable” designation for Saturday.

Burkle and Tatsch, meanwhile, are “doubtful.”

title: No.13 Penn State women’s volleyball set for Wrigley Field matchup with No. 3 Kentucky
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions arrive off of a successful Penn State Invitational performance, sweeping its opponents in two out of its three wins throughout the weekend. Up next, the blue and white will travel to play No. 3 Kentucky at Wrigley Field.

The Nittany Lions beat both Hofstra and UConn 3-0, while also escaping with a 3-2 win in a gritty battle with High Point.

After a long awaited debut, Alexis Stucky finished her first appearance in a blue and white uniform with 27 assists, six blocks, nine digs and an ace against UConn.

Stucky was not the only one making her first Happy Valley appearance. Freshman Danielle Whitmire also saw playing time, putting up five assists to aid the Nittany Lions in their sweep victory.

Graduate student outside hitter Whitney Lauenstein put up big numbers this weekend, leading the blue and white in its final two wins against High Point and Hofstra. Lauenstein totaled three digs and 14 digs against Hofstra and contributed three aces and six kills in the win against High Point.

Going into the match against Kentucky, the Stucky-Launstein duo will be dangerous. Kennedy Martin, senior right side hitter, was named MVP of the Invitational, after she added 17 kills, and three aces while hitting over .500.

Kentucky has played five games so far, only losing once to Pittsburgh with a score of 3-1. Each of their wins has been a sweep.

Heading into Sunday, Kentucky last faced UCLA, where they dominated 3-0. A large portion of their offense against the Bruins was aided by their stunning seven aces.

Notre Dame transfer Morgan Gaerte led the Wildcats in the sweep, 16 kills. Senior outside hitter Brooklyn DeLeye added onto Gaerte’s hits, pairing 15 kills of her own.

This isn’t the first time the Gaerte-DeLeye duo has come together to dominate the Wildcat offense. In Kentucky’s season opener against Wisconsin, the pair combined for a total of 22 kills to sweep the Badgers.

The Gaerte-Delaye tag team could pose a competitive front against Penn State’s Stucky-Martin duo backed by Lauenstein.

Kentucky is putting forth a very similar squad to last year, only losing one significant player, outside hitter Eva Hudson. Other than that, experience and chemistry is rooted in Kentucky’s starting line as Asia Thigpen, Georgia Watson, Hannah Benjamin and Bellamie Beus are all returning.

Because of this, SEC conference coaches favored Kentucky to win the SEC title for the tenth time this year.

On the contrary, Penn State is reshaping a partly new squad, with a balanced mix of returners and newcomers. The blue and white are welcoming seven new players, including four freshmen and three transfers; the most notable transfer being Stucky, a long-time teammate of Martin at Florida.

The seven newcomers will be joined by notable returners including Martin, Emmi Sellman, Caroline Jurevicius and Gabrielle Nichols.

In program history, the Nittany Lions have seen the Wildcats a total of eight times so far, as Penn State won seven of the meetups. While history is on Penn State's side, the most recent match, just last year, was taken by Kentucky.

The Wildcats traveled to University Park almost exactly a year ago from when they were set to play on Sunday. Kentucky won this match in a sweep. The blue and white were outplayed in kills, aces, digs, assists and blocks.

title: Where to find Penn State's local music scene
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s local music scene has exploded within the last few years. Not only has the scene become a place for homegrown acts to flourish, but it's slowly becoming a staple destination for local bands and artists from other college towns wanting to expand their fanbase.

Today’s typical concert experience consists of monopolies like Ticketmaster skyrocketing their prices, sliding in obscene hidden fees at the last second, all for you to sit in bumper-to-bumper traffic on your way to pay $45 for a parking spot in the dusty, back corner of a lot.

Once you’re finally in the stadium, you’re hemorrhaging your bank account for a pretzel and a bottle of water — just to sit in the nosebleeds while your favorite band plays on the other side of the stadium.

So, what are students starting to do in lieu of not having the budget for a big name concert? They’re turning to their own local music scene.

At Penn State, the community around the streets of venues on College and Beaver Avenue are not just fans of music, but of watching their peers and their friends get on stage and give the whole crowd a night they wished they could repeat.

Manny’s

The first pit stop for anyone looking to get more invested in the local scene is Manny’s Live Performance Space. Since early 2025, this all-ages club has been a go-to venue for any band or musician looking for a fun, open space to display their talents and put on a great show.

As you descend the stairs into the main area, you’re greeted with the poised faces of music legends like Bob Dylan, Lou Reed and Frank Zappa plastered on the walls. Then, you enter the low-lit, wood-paneled room. The stage is low and the floor can get just tight enough to where you can feel the energy of the crowd, but you’re not sweating in a claustrophobic panic, allowing you to be fully immersed in the band you went to see.

According to Manny's website, it’s “ designed for those who value creativity, connection and meaningful hospitality.” The attendees of these late night, underground, musical rendezvous surely live up to that statement.

Every person in attendance at these shows is moving and grooving no matter who’s up on stage. It’s pure energy and acceptance all around.

Movin’ On

For those not looking to pay for tickets, there are many fraternities around campus that will often host local bands to play for functions during the year.

Another huge event for student acts and fans of local music is the Movin’ On BATTLE and subsequent Movin’ On Festival. At the Movin’ On BATTLE, a handful of student bands and artists are selected to compete for the opening slot of Penn State’s Movin’ On Festival.

Last year’s festival included Slayyyter and Zara Larsson — so you can catch some big names all for the humble price of $0.

Mojofest

Back in April 2026, Penn State held its first ever Mojofest Happy Valley, another huge step in cultivating a community of local and student bands. It was the first time the festival had been held at a campus outside of Massachusetts.

Mojofest is a chapter of Local Mojo, an Amherst, Massachusetts-based organization started in 2021. April’s event featured several young bands and DJs from the Penn State area.

Local Mojo has helped student bands across six different chapters find performance spaces, promotion, media and anything else that will help more people come out and watch a show.

Now, while there are several places and events for you to see live bands, let's find out just exactly who’s playing around town.

Local bands

Some of the most popular acts brought up in Happy Valley are killer bands like Sarasota, Amelia and Sequoia (last year's Movin’ On BATTLE winners), the hard-rocking trio Tuck&Roll, Ham on a Stick and 346 Sunrise. And those are just a few of the well-beloved Penn State groups that are starting to make a name for themselves both in and out of State College.

What’s so great about Penn State’s local scene is that it’s incredibly welcoming and exciting for other underground acts to come through and play alongside some of the more local groups. Bands like the popular Amherst, Massachusetts three-piece Morrissey Blvd, the Harrisburg-based Jay Veil and SKORTS all the way from Brooklyn.

By and large, Penn State’s passion and commitment to supporting local music will only grow more and more from here on out. People have a taste of what it’s like to head down to Manny’s or stop by a frat house to see a few of their friends get on stage and give them a loud night full of jams and laughs.
