title: Position preview | Penn State RBs bring plethora of depth
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
When it comes to the running back position this year, Penn State has the difficult task of replacing the production of two of its all-time greats.

Both Nick Singleton and Kaytron Allen are in the NFL, and with added talent from the transfer portal, it could be a running back by committee look rather than one or two backs standing out on the field.

Here’s how the running back room could shape up in Savon Huggins’ first year as coach.

Expected leaders

The Nittany Lions could have upward of four running backs making an impact this season, of which two are returners and two are transfers.

Ohio State transfer James Peoples and Iowa State transfer Carson Hansen are the two names expected to get a brunt of the work.

Peoples dealt with a crowded running back room at Ohio State, rushing for 344 yards on 61 carries in 2025. As the season went along, Peoples saw his playing time diminish with the emergence of then-true freshman Bo Jackson.

Peoples’ work in the offseason has allowed him to become more of a true all-around back in his eyes, something that could help him see the field more often.

Hansen has the most experience of any running back in the room as one of the lead backs the last two years with the Cyclones.

Last season, he just missed the 1,000-yard mark, with 952 rushing yards and six touchdowns. Hansen’s ability to be in the game during short-yardage situations can allow him to see the field often no matter which running back is standing out.

Returning depth

The Nittany Lions have two key returners at running back in Quinton Martin Jr. and Cam Wallace, both of which could work themselves into the top running back situation.

Martin emerged as a potential top running back with his breakout performance in the Prinstripe Bowl. The WPIAL product showcased why he was a composite 4-star out of high school, with 20 rushes for 103 yards. Martin’s strengths as a pass catcher will play a major factor in his playing time this season.

Wallace, on the other hand, dealt with serious injuries in 2024 that left him unavailable for the rest of the season. Wallace has played in just four career games, with a career high of 39 rushing yards coming against Kent State in 2024, the game he broke bones in both of his legs.

Freshmen

Penn State has three freshmen behind the four top running backs, headlined by State College native D’Ante Sheffey.

Sheffey committed to Penn State in January after decommitting from Syracuse on Nov. 23, joining the growing 2026 recruiting class at the time. The freshman has made strides in his first year and could set himself up for playing time after this season.

Joining him in the room is 3-star Amar’e Glover, who stands around the same size as Sheffey, at 6 feet, 205 pounds. Glover didn’t sign anywhere in December and committed to Penn State as a preferred walk-on out of Delaware.

Alongside Glover as a preferred walk-on is Jeremy Washington. The 5-foot-9 running back joined the Nittany Lions from Gonzaga College High School, the same high school of former Penn State tackle Olu Fashanu.

title: Line dancing, silent disco, and more | Happening in the Valley
author: Colleen Cratty | The Daily Collegian
description:
With the fun of sylly week now over, assignments are racking up and schedules are overflowing. But Happy Valley has many events for you to decompress, relax or even have some fun. These events are a great way to find some balance and get back into the swing of things at Penn State.

Here’s what’s happening in the Valley in the coming week.

Monday, Aug. 31

Yoga and Meditation

If you’re looking for some relaxing exercise on Monday night, this free Yoga and Meditation class is a great choice. The session is led by a certified instructor and all the poses can be adapted to your comfort level and ability, which makes it perfect for beginners.

Health Promotion and Wellness hosts these classes multiple times a week all over campus. Materials are limited, so you might want to bring your own.

The class is in the Memorial Lounge of the Pasquerilla Spiritual Center from 5 to 6 p.m.

Tuesday, Sept. 1

Nature Sketching

The Penn State Arboretum plans many events to enjoy the outdoors during every season. This activity is perfect for students who love both art and nature.

Located in the Overlook Pavillion and held from 10 to 11:30 a.m., you can either bring your own sketchbook and art supplies or use ones provided by the Arboretum. The event wraps up with participants optionally sharing their artwork with the rest of the class.

Boalsburg Farmer’s Market

For an option outside of State College, the Boalsburg Farmer’s Market is held every Tuesday. The market has fresh fruit, vegetables, meat and fish as well as local food and drink vendors.

Some unique options to try are kombucha stands, wood-fired pizza and tamales. One stand sells homemade frozen meals, which are a great option for college students who are too busy to cook or without a kitchen. As for non-food items, you can get flower arrangements or even CBD products.

You can visit the market at 113 East Pine St. every Tuesday from 2 to 6 p.m.

Involvement Fair

A crucial event for anyone looking to get involved on campus is the annual Involvement Fair. Different types of clubs crowd the HUB-Robeson Center lawn looking for new members (and sometimes bribe you with candy to join their GroupMe). It's a great time to explore what organizations have to offer, learn about others’ experiences and discover ways to join options like club sports and Greek life.

The Involvement Fair is a great way to get involved with THON organizations as well. These groups have already started raising money in preparation for the February 2027 event, but it's never too late to join the cause.

Besides the wider known organizations, there are so many unique groups that you can learn about and sign up to join at the fair. It’ll take place on the HUB-Robeson lawn on Tuesday, Sept. 1, and Wednesday, Sept. 2, from 12 to 5 p.m.

Wednesday, Sept. 2

Don Toliver concert

The Bryce Jordan Center will host hip-hop sensation Don Toliver for his Nitrous Octane World Tour on Wednesday. Following the extreme success of his most recent album, Octane, he’s bringing the second leg of his tour to State College. The concert setlist consists of his hit songs, including TikTok viral “E85.”

Student tickets are sold out, but standard admission is still available on Ticketmaster.

Doors open at 6:30 p.m. and the show starts at 7:30 p.m.

Thursday, Sept. 3

Good Times Line Dancing Company’s Country Night

If you’re looking to bring a southern country feel to State College, Happy Valley Live hosts Good Times Line Dancing Company’s Country Night every Thursday.

The event consists of line dances for all levels of experience, so it's perfect for those who want to try something new. They weave in lessons throughout the night, so beginners can learn dances with some help. It also features a mechanical bull and drink specials for those over 21.

The event is hosted at Happy Valley Live in State College from 6 to 9 p.m. every Thursday.

Friday, Sept. 4

Back to State Fun Friday

Penn State’s Black Caucus, Latino Caucus, Asian Pacific Islander Desi American (APIDA) Caucus, and the Paul Robeson Cultural Center (PRCC) will host their first welcome event on Friday.

If you’re looking to get involved with one of the caucuses or just want an activity to look forward to during the school day, it’s a great option. They’re providing free food in the form of a multicultural cookout, as well as numerous activities. There’s henna, balloon twisting, a photo booth and more. The event’s music is provided by DJ DB Soundz.

Back to State Fun Friday takes place in the Heritage Hall in the HUB from 12 to 2 p.m.

Silent Disco

Another good nature outing is the Silent Disco, held in the Arboretum’s Childhood’s Gate Children’s Garden. They provide glowing, wireless headphones with multiple live DJ channels to flip through. It’s great for anyone who wants to choose their own adventure, because you can pick the volume and the music.

While you enjoy the music, you can view the beautiful nature in the Arboretum. The event is free, open to everyone and from 7 to 10 p.m. on Friday.

title: Local, state groups hold town hall to plan advocacy for data center regulations
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
Dozens gathered at the Boalsburg Fire Hall on Sunday for a town hall to plan next steps for advocacy for increased data center regulations in Centre County and across Pennsylvania.

The town hall had speakers from Central PA United, its sister chapter Voice of Westmoreland (VOW), No Data Centers in Mifflin County and Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania. The organizations’ presentations focused on their efforts to either actively oppose proposals for hyperscale AI data centers in communities, or pass regulations for their development.

Hyperscale data centers, which are characterized by campuses spanning several buildings across a wide area of land, have been adopted by developers to fulfill the needs of artificial intelligence, expanding its capabilities to store and process data. A 2025 report by Data Center Watch said the reasons communities oppose hyperscale data centers include preventing higher utility bills, increased water consumption and noise pollution, and the impact on property value and green space preservation.

While there are no proposals for hyperscale data center proposals in Centre County, Central PA United organizer Robert Zeigler said it was important for local governments to still pursue strong data center regulations — which is what he’s working on as vice president of the Millheim Borough Council.

Zeigler said there’s a need for community members to remain informed on what they can do to assist in the push for regulating data centers.

“With a lot of the actions happening across the state regarding AI data centers and the potential damages they could do to local communities, we're trying to educate people, engage them and then get them to be empowered to take action locally and statewide to mitigate the risks while maximizing the opportunity to protect their communities,” Zeigler said.

For Greenburg resident and Voice of Westmoreland organizer Rose Piern, the issue of data centers is a real one as she has helped to rally support to oppose projects in Allegheny County’s Springdale and Westmoreland County’s Upper Burrell Township.

Zeigler said one of the challenges faced by VOW in opposing these projects are nondisclosure agreements, which limit how much information about the proposals is available once signed.

“They've been fighting not just the AI data centers environmentally, but also the fact that they're not being transparent,” Zeigler said. “The public is being blindsided by it.”

Piern said the proposal of a data center can be enticing for some local governments, specifically in the Rust Belt, who have struggled to obtain funding for services following deindustrialization.

“You have a lot of very desperate communities that are starving for income to keep the streets paved and the trash picked up and the buildings in working order, et cetera,” Piern said. “They're very vulnerable to big, billion-dollar companies coming in and saying, ‘We will fix all your problems by giving you a better tax base, by bringing in jobs.’”

She said she hopes events like the town hall lead to a statewide coalition that calls for more politicians in Harrisburg to enact data center regulations in the commonwealth, especially from state senators Kim Ward and Joe Pittman who are preventing sessions for discussion of or actively opposing the passing of this legislation.

Following the conclusion of presentations, attendees split up into groups to collaborate on ways they could better advocate against data centers and for regulation at the local and state level.

Dennis Hsieh, of Patton Township, said the conversations among his group began looking at State College, but expanded outward as there wasn’t enough land left in the borough for a hyperscale data center proposal.

Hsieh, a Central PA United member, said one of his group’s topics was combatting the dismissal by data center developers of community members’ concerns.

“We don't want these hyperscale data centers of this degree to affect our way of living. That we have to pay more bills, we have to worry about contaminated water, we have to worry about the temperature rises from the water being dumped because the water is being used to cool the data centers,” Hsieh said.

He said much of the public is still unaware as to what exactly hyperscale data centers are, and what impacts they have on the community.

“We need to educate people on what these things are before they can understand how they take action or if they need to decide they won't take action,” Hsieh said. “I think that's the most important part, that we need to educate the people on what hyperscale data centers are and what their effects are in the environment.”

title: Penn State women’s volleyball earns sweep behind complete team performance
author: Lily Dorf | The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 10 Penn State Nittany Lions returned to Rec Hall at 6 p.m. for the final match of the Penn State Invitational, capping the undefeated homestand in spectacular fashion.

The Nittany Lions took on Hofstra, winning 25-23 to secure a three-match sweep after wins against Connecticut and High Point. Over the entire stretch, the blue and white dropped only a pair of sets, both in the morning clash against the Panthers. Despite starting the day slow, Penn State fired on all cylinders in the nightcap against the Pride, with seemingly no holes in the squad's game.

“High Point pushed us really well this morning,” Ava Falduto said. “But we knew we had more to give tonight, so we made sure to rest and get our film in, and then be ready for tonight's match.”

Penn State began with fire against Hofstra, forcing the Pride into an early timeout after falling behind by four. After dropping the first set of the day to High Point, the Nittany Lions wouldn’t succumb to the same fate, as they closed it out 25-20.

“We did lots of film treatment and recovery,” Ryla Jones said. “I think, like after the first match (against High Point), we just regrouped and kind of had some goals that we wanted to make sure we accomplished in the next one”

The blue and white kept the form rolling into the second frame, securing the set in the most dominant fashion it has done so far this young season. Hofstra had no answer for the Penn State attack led by Kennedy Martin and Whitney Lauenstein, who combined on the day for 31 kills and four of five of the Nittany Lions aces.

“Whit takes some big swings, and she's got the green light,” coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley said. "I think we can help her find ways to manage the ball a little bit more, but you know she's aggressive and wants to score and wants the ball a lot and you know I'm glad she's on her side of the net”

Serving stood as a main key to the blue and white’s victory, as it also limited Hofstra’s ability to get points from the end line.

“We serve every day, and you know I thought Ryla had a good weekend serving,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “Just being aggressive from the end line and finding other ways to score and get them off the net. So I thought we did a nice job of serving aggressively all weekend.”

With a trio of wins under its belt at its home invitational, Penn State begins an early-season resume scattered with optimism and time in the spotlight after the Spikes Under the Lights exhibition to begin the season. The Nittany Lions continue that trend when they leave Happy Valley for Chicago to play in the historic Wrigley Field against a formidable Kentucky squad.

“It was a tournament with some really good teams. It was nice to see us finish on a win and see everyone contribute to the team's success.”

title: Penn State women’s volleyball cruises to sweep over Hofstra in final match of Penn State Invitational
author: Elliott Inscho | Sports Editor
description:
Penn State vanquished High Point in a five-set slugfest on Sunday morning, but victory came a whole lot easier in their second match of the day against Hofstra.

Kennedy Martin and Whitney Lauenstein combined for 31 kills in an efficient sweep of the Pride, and helped to keep the Nittany Lions undefeated through the first three matches of the regular season.

Martin, a reigning All-American outside hitter, got the match started with a kill after recording six in Sunday's earlier match against High Point. Hofstra rebounded quickly with a three-point run, and the Nittany Lions ripped off two of their own to tie the set at 3-3.

Gabrielle Nichols and Haley Burgdorf delivered smooth swings that found the floor for Penn State points, but the Pride kept things neck-and-neck early in the set until they surrendered four straight points, including one where two players collided and let the ball fall softly to the court.

Nichols’ second kill of the set forced a timeout from Hofstra coach Emily Mansur. The Pride looked stronger coming out of it, alternating points with the blue and white, but a blistering four-point streak by Penn State gave them a 15-8 lead as the set entered the media timeout.

After Martin found the first kill after the break, Hofstra fired off a five-point run that lessened the Penn State lead to three before setter Alexis Stucky caught the Pride off guard with a quick tap over the net.

The Nittany Lions won four of the next six points to extend their lead in the set’s dying stages slowly. A serve from Martin sailed past the back line and a three-point Hofstra run was sparked.

Martin bounced back with her sixth and seventh kills to send the blue and white to set point, quickly eclipsing her total from the five-set battle with High Point a few hours earlier.

Beatriz Braga powered a serve of her own out-of-bounds, and the first set went to Penn State.

The blue and white carried momentum into the second set, claiming five of the opening six points, four of which came on kills from Whitney Lauenstein.

Sonja Rundcrantz couldn’t find the court with her serve, and Martin delivered an ace in response to put the Nittany Lions up 8-3. The five-point edge led Mansur to call her second timeout of the match, but it proved futile.

Penn State continued to overpower the Pride, as Martin delivered strong service that was too much for them to handle. She made two more aces, and Kendall Northern notched a kill of her own to finish up a seven-point run that swelled the Nittany Lion lead to 13-3.

Trailing heavily, Hofstra managed a four-point run of their own to get back within striking distance in the set. Penn State halted it with a trio in response, and after a single score from the Pride, the blue and white fired off six straight to take a commanding 23-9 lead.

A bad set by the Pride saw a ball fall harmlessly to the court and usher in set point. Stucky’s serve was rallied back and forth, the Nittany Lions keeping play alive with several digs, until Martin’s powerful swing clinched the frame for Penn State.

The blue and white went on an eight-point run to end the set and, after an opening point from Hofstra, notched five straight to start the third frame.

Lauenstein and Martin delivered back-to-back kills, the tenth of the match for both of them. The 6-foot-6 Martin then combined with Ryla Jones before another block by Jones and Finley Krystkowiak led to a timeout by the Pride.

Hofstra got the first point after the break on a service error from Lauenstein. Jones delivered a smooth swing before Martin made two more kills, leading the Pride to use their final timeout of the night.

This one proved to be slightly more effective than those preceding it, as it initiated a slight two-point run, but the ever-inevitable Martin made kill No. 13 to end it. Not to be outdone, Lauenstein got her eleventh soon after.

Hofstra battled back, cutting the lead down to four points on a three-point run, but Martin’s fifteenth kill shut the streak down. Alternating points followed the emphatic swing, until the Pride narrowed Penn State’s lead to 19-16.

Lauenstein’s thirteenth kill helped to re-strengthen the advantage to five points, but Hofstra won three consecutive scores to make it a two-point game late. She made another before an ace from Stucky gave them a seemingly insurmountable four-point lead.

Mansur successfully challenged an attack error from her squad that appeared to bring the contest to match point, and her squad won the ensuing two points to cut Penn State’s lead to 23-22.

Yet another forceful swing by Martin resulted in a true match point, and after a service error by Lauenstein, she made No. 17 to seal the victory for the blue and white.

Up next

Penn State will travel to Chicago, where they’ll play Kentucky in a big-time matchup at Wrigley Field. The match in the Friendly Confines is set to begin at 7 p.m., and will be nationally broadcast on FOX.

title: Nikki Crane's hat trick fuels Penn State women's soccer in win over Brown
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
It was a special one in Happy Valley on Sunday as Penn State women's soccer celebrated their seniors in a whopping 6-0 Senior Day victory against Brown.

Seniors Mackenzie Gress, Kayleigh Herr, Paige Kalal, Kaelyn Wolf and Molly Martin were honored pregame before the victory.

1st half

Penn State looked to continue the momentum after a 5-0 victory against Bucknell, and they did just that. The Nittany Lions started the game in possession of the ball well in Brown's final third with lots of duels won and shots on goal, but no real big chances came until Bella Ayscue provided a perfectly weighted pass to freshman Ellie Kocher, who put a saved shot on goal. In the 27th minute, Lily Boyden received a ball from the other side of the box, cut inside and drew a penalty for the blue and white.

Ayscue stepped up for the penalty and slotted it in the bottom left corner to give Penn State the 1-0 lead. The Nittany Lions continued to possess the ball, suffocating Brown whenever they tried to attack the midfield. In the 38th minute, Penn State's Olivia Robinson won a loose ball in Brown's final third; she then proceeded to chip Brown's goalkeeper and gave redshirt freshman Nicole Crane a tap-in opportunity that she put in the back of the net to make the score 2-0 for Penn State. The goal marked a milestone in Crane's career, being her first collegiate goal. Penn State later found more fortune when it won a free kick in the 41st minute. Ayscue stepped up to take it, where she found the head of Crane, who headed it in for her second goal of the match, giving Penn State a commanding 3-0 lead heading into halftime.

2nd half

Penn State continued its dominance to begin the second half with the blue and white holding most possession. With 41 minutes left to go, the Nittany Lions won a corner kick and sent the ball to Kocher; she fired a well-paced shot on target, but the Brown goalkeeper saved it. This didn’t discourage Kocher because with 36 minutes to go, she received a pass from Aubrey Kulpa on the right side of the pitch. She then proceeded to let it rip from just outside of the box, putting it across goal to give the Nittany Lions a 4-0 lead. The goal marks the first collegiate goal of Kocher's career, who served as Penn State's chance creator for most of the game. Later in the second half, Brown appeared to have the ball and looked more comfortable creating chances in Penn State's final third; ultimately, nothing materialized. Penn State then caught fire, scoring two goals in the 80th minute, with the first being scored by Lilly Burger, assisted by Paige Pasinski and the second scored by Crane, giving her a hat trick on the day. It was a breakout day for Crane as she came into the game with zero collegiate goals to her name and exited with three.

Penn State looked dominant in this match, and Brown didn't get many chances. It seemed like every time they tried to possess in the midfield, the Nittany Lions were always right there to fight for the ball back. In the last two matches, Penn State has outscored opponents 11-0, showing that the team could be a problem for opposing sides in the Big Ten this season.

Up next

Penn State's Next fixture will be against Virginia Tech on Thursday in Happy Valley

title: Former Penn State QB Will Levis waived by Tennessee Titans
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
A former Penn State quarterback has been cut.

Will Levis was waived by the Tennessee Titans on Sunday, per Tom Pelissero.

The former Nittany Lion played two seasons with the Titans, throwing for 3,899 yards, 21 touchdowns and 16 interceptions.

Levis played at Penn State from 2018-20 primarily as the backup. He appeared in 15 games in his career with a single start before transferring to Kentucky.

After two seasons at Kentucky, Levis was drafted No. 33 overall in the 2023 NFL Draft. He was the Titans' starting quarterback in 2024.

title: Penn State field hockey seize 1st win of the season, Hannah Prince era
author: Owen Lomotan I The Daily Collegian
description:
After a 4-3 overtime loss in their season opener against the Virginia Cavaliers on Friday, August 28, the Nittany Lions looked to bounce back and earn their first win of the 2026 season against the Lock Haven Bald Eagles on Sunday, August 30.

The blue and white found themselves in a tight battle until the end.

Penn State’s offense wasted no time getting started. Freshman forward Chloe D’Hage’s early tip attempt was stopped by a Bald Eagle deflection two minutes in.

The Nittany Lion offense produced several shots throughout the opening minutes of the contest, but the Lock Haven defense held firm and none were on target.

The blue and white’s first penalty corner came with 9:14 left in the first quarter. Sophomore midfielder Joji Purdy’s shot went high, and the score remained 0-0.

The Bald Eagles gained their first penalty chances with 4:51 and 4:42 remaining in the opening quarter. Both times, the blue and white defense held the attack back.

Senior midfielder Natalie Freeman’s quick strike with 3:23 remaining was sent back immediately by Lock Haven sophomore goalie Quinty van Luijk.

In the final seconds, Purdy’s shot was Penn State’s closest chance at a goal, but it was unsuccessful.

The score remained 0-0 after the first quarter. The Nittany Lions took seven shots, Lock Haven’s van Luijk stopping them all.

To open the second quarter, junior forward Ella Gaitan’s shot was blocked by van Luijk once again.

Sophomore forward Olivia Marthins got Penn State on the board first with a quick shot in the box with 12:46 to go in the half, giving the Nittany Lions a 1-0 lead.

The blue and white’s second penalty corner was called with 10:46 to go in the second. The call was overturned on further review and ruled a faceoff in Lock Haven territory.

The Bald Eagles were given their second penalty corner of the game with 9:04 remaining in the first half. Lock Haven came up short after Nittany Lion junior goalie Aby Deverka blocked it cleanly.

Redshirt freshman Hope Russo’s spin shot was unsuccessful, but it prompted another penalty corner for Penn State with just over six minutes to go in the first half.

The Nittany Lions came up short of a second goal after Gaitan’s shot was off target.

The blue and white earned yet another penalty corner with 4:23 remaining in the opening half. Penn State freshman forward Lilly Holmes’s shot off the corner missed the target, and the score remained 1-0.

A yellow card was given to Lock Haven freshman midfielder Maggie Moylan with just 35 seconds left in the half, which gave her a four-minute, thirty-second penalty to start the second half.

The second quarter closed with the Nittany Lions holding a narrow 1-0 lead.

The third quarter kicked off with an early blue and white penalty corner with 12:33 remaining, but it was unsuccessful.

Penn State was given a penalty stroke by graduate forward Sienna Dunn with 12:23 left. Dunn scored, giving the Nittany Lions a 2-0 lead.

Penn State scored once again only seconds later with a shot from D’Hage with 11:44 remaining, giving the Nittany Lions a 3-0 lead.

The blue and white penalty corner at 11:07 was unsuccessful, yet the pressure was felt for the Lock Haven defense.

The Bald Eagle penalty corner at 10:07 was deflected away, and no score resulted.

With 6:29 remaining in the third quarter, the Nittany Lions were given another penalty corner, and the shot went wide from junior forward Katelyn Strawser.

With 5:25 left, Penn State scored once again, this time from Russo, giving the blue and white a 4-0 lead.

The Nittany Lions were given a seventh penalty corner with 2:54 remaining in the 3rd. The shot from Purdy was successful and Penn State led 5-0.

Penn State was given another penalty corner with 1:36 left in the quarter, resulting in several close calls but no score.

The blue and white penalty corner with 1:16 left resulted in a goal for the Nittany Lions, with Purdy being the beneficiary of the initial deflection.

Heading into the fourth, the blue and white were comfortably in front with a 6-0 lead, five of those goals being in the third period alone.

The Nittany Lions opened the final quarter with a seventh goal from Freeman with 14:36 remaining in the game.

Penn State was given another penalty corner with 6:26 to go and Gaitan scored again, pushing the lead up to eight goals for the blue and white.

The blue and white ended their second game of the season with an impressive 8-0 win over the Bald Eagles, matching their 2025 total against Lock Haven last season.

“It was awesome to be able to rotate all of our field players through the game and get everyone an opportunity to play because the girls have been working so hard since we started August 7,” coach Hannah Prince said. “I’m really proud of their effort and getting themselves refocused at halftime, which is important.”

“After halftime, we just really focused on implementing a couple changes but also just playing to our standard. We set it in the fourth quarter verses UVA and that has to be what we go for every single day” Prince said.

Up next

The next two games for the Nittany Lions are at home Friday against the Villanova Wildcats at 3 p.m. and Sunday against the Delaware Blue Hens at 12 p.m.

title: Former Penn State WR Trebor Peña released by Jacksonville Jaguars
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
The wave of cuts has begun in the NFL.

Former Penn State wide receiver Trebor Peña was waived by the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday, according to Jordan Schultz. The Jaguars hope to bring him back on the practice squad.

Peña was signed by the Jaguars as an undrafted free agent on April 26, with an attempt to make the team out of training camp.

The former Nittany Lion made a case for himself in the preseason, catching seven passes for 91 yards and a touchdown throughout three games.

Peña played one season with the Nittany Lions after transferring from Syracuse, totaling 552 yards and two touchdowns during the 2025 season. He was a standout in Penn State's Pinstripe Bowl victory over Clemson, catching five passes for 100 yards and a touchdown.

If Peña returns to the Jaguars on the practice squad, he'll remain with former Nittany Lions Parker Washington and Brenton Strange in Jacksonville.

title: 3 former Penn State players released by Baltimore Ravens
author: Andrew Deal & Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
As NFL rosters are being trimmed down to 53 players, two former Penn Staters have been released.

Center Nick Dawkins, edge rusher Adisa Isaac and linebacker Dom DeLuca were all released by the Baltimore Ravens.

Dawkins signed with the Ravens as an undrafted free agent, but didn't do enough to make the 53-man roster.

The former Nittany Lion spent five seasons in Happy Valley, including his last two as the starting center. In 2025, he was named All-Big Ten Honorable Mention in addition to his role as team captain.

Isaac was drafted in the third round of the 2024 NFL Draft by the Ravens, but couldn't consistently find the field.

The former Penn Stater played in just four games in 2024 and didn't see the field the rest of the time. In 2025, Isaac was placed on injured reserve after getting surgery to repair a dislocated elbow.

Isaac started in every game in his final two years in Happy Valley, totaling 11.5 sacks from 2022-23.

DeLuca was a standout in the Ravens' dominant 41-3 win over the Washington Commanders on Friday, tallying eight tackles to lead the team.

DeLuca notched 12 tackles across the Ravens' three preseason games, but didn't do enough to make his way onto the initial roster.

At Penn State, DeLuca was one of the team's leaders, showing out on special teams in addition to his defensive efforts. His most productive game came in the Nittany Lions' opening game of the College Football Playoff against SMU, with two interceptions, one being returned for a touchdown.

Baltimore is still home to two Nittany Lions in Vega Ioane and Amani Oruwariye.

title: No. 10 Penn State women's volleyball outlasts High Point over five sets
author: Elliott Inscho | Sports Editor
description:
Penn State served up a win for breakfast on Sunday.

In an early-morning tilt, the Nittany Lions survived a late scare and took down High Point in five sets, remaining unblemished in the young season.

A tone-setting block by Kennedy Martin was the catalyst for a 5-2 Penn State run to open the first set, a stretch that ushered in a High Point timeout after freshman middle blocker Kendall Northern made a powerful swing to secure the fifth point.

Right out of the timeout, Gabrielle Nichols found a gap in the Panthers’ defense for an ace. High Point ended the three-point run by Penn State on a kill from Talia Lardner immediately to follow.

The Panthers went on a three-point run of their own, narrowing the Nittany Lions’ lead to a single score. Penn State won back-to-back points to widen the gap, but a dominant High Point run saw them earn six consecutive points to take a 12-9 lead.

Martin finally got the Nittany Lions back on track with her second kill of the set, before a four-point streak from the blue and white put them back ahead with a one-point lead.

The Panthers won consecutive points to regain a 15-14 advantage. The teams alternated points to keep things close down the stretch, but a combined block of Whitney Lauenstein’s swing saw High Point hold a 21-19 lead late.

Down by three, Katie Schumacher-Cawley called her first timeout of the match in an attempt to settle things, but an ace by Bukovcan and attack error by Martin capped a four-point run that clinched the first set for High Point.

Penn State rebounded to open the second frame, going on a 4-1 run to start it. A Burgdorf block forced another early-set timeout from High Point coach Ryan Meek, which resulted in a pair of points for his squad before Martin delivered another powerful kill.

Errors by the Panthers and an ace from Martin fueled a three-point run by Penn State, which forced Meek to utilize his second timeout of the set with the Nittany Lions leading 9-4.

After the break, the 6-foot-6 senior made her second ace of the set to stretch her squad’s lead to seven points. High Point scored three straight, but a four-point run by the blue and white erased their progress and put them up by eight.

Penn State’s service stayed hot, as libero Ava Falduto delivered consecutive aces in the midst of a 6-0 run by the Nittany Lions. The Panthers went on a four-point streak to keep things interesting late, but it wasn’t enough to keep the blue and white from securing a 25-13 victory in a juxtaposing second set.

In almost the exact same opening as the second frame, Meek called a timeout after Penn State jumped out to another 4-1 lead in the third. High Point allowed two quick points out of the break before Meek called for another.

Down by six, the Panthers won two straight points before the Nittany Lions responded with three. A kill and emphatic block by Elodie Lalonde, followed by an ace by Sydney McKay, sparked six straight points by High Point that brought them within one, before Nichols stopped the bleeding.

Ryla Jones made her fourth ace of the match coming out of the media timeout to give Penn State a 16-13 edge. After a kill by the Panthers, a four-point run by the Nittany Lions put them up by six in the closing stages.

High Point won five of seven points to tighten things up, but a four-point run finished by a Burgdorf kill won Penn State the third set.

Caroline Jurevicius made a pair of kills and the Panthers made a pair of errors as the blue and white took a 6-3 lead in the beginning of the fourth frame. Another error and a kill by Burgdorf forced Meek to call for a break with Penn State up by five.

The Nittany Lions won four of six points to follow, stretching their lead to seven. Four straight service errors saw the teams alternate scores, but kills by Finley Krystkowiak and Emmi Sellman fueled a run where Penn State won four of five to take a ten-point lead.

High Point battled late, with three straight kills opening a five-point run that cut the lead to just five. An intense rally looked to end the run with a Sellman kill, but a lengthy review flipped the call in favor of the Panthers on a net violation.

The streak stretched to eight, cutting the Penn State advantage to just two points, until Sellman got her kill to end it. High Point won two more points to cut the Penn State lead to 20-19 after the Panthers were down 19-10 earlier in the set.

They tied it up at 21-21 when Bukovcan made an ace, and Schumacher-Cawley called her first timeout since the first set. High Point took the lead immediately after, and back-to-back service errors brought its advantage to 23-22.

A service error from Jurevicius led to a High Point set point, but Krystkowiak made a kill to extend the match. A service error of her own afterwards gave the Panthers another opportunity, which they capitalized on with a Lardner kill to send the match to the fifth set.

Early in the shortened fifth set, the Nittany Lions took a quick 5-1 advantage after a kill from Jones and two aces by Lauenstein. Krystkowiak got her ninth kill of the match before another ace from Jones resulted in a High Point timeout with the Panthers down 8-3.

Meek’s squad won back-to-back points before they committed four consecutive errors to put Penn State up by seven. They responded, though, delivering two kills back-to-back aces to bring themselves within three.

The Panthers won another point before Martin’s powerful swing rebounded off of a High Point back-liner and into the Rec Hall stands.

A Nichols kill resulted in match point, and an assertive Lauenstein kill brought the grueling, five-set marathon to a close, giving the Nittany Lions their second victory.

Up next

Penn State will go for an undefeated weekend when they face Hofstra at 6 p.m. in the final match of the Penn State Invitational. The match can be streamed on B1G+.

title: No. 10 Penn State women’s volleyball sweeps UConn in Rec Hall opener
author: Elliott Inscho | Sports Editor
description:
Volleyball season is officially back in Happy Valley, and Penn State opened its 2026 campaign with a bang.

The Nittany Lions cruised to a three-set sweep over UConn on Saturday, opening the regular season on the right foot after falling to SMU in an exhibition during the Spikes Under the Lights tournament.

“It was a great crowd tonight,” Katie Schumacher-Cawley said. “It's always nice to win. It's hard to win, and I thought we did a nice job. Collectively as a team, we did some nice things.”

Alexis Stucky electrified a roaring Rec Hall crowd early in her home debut, winning consecutive points on a block and ace to open the first set. After UConn won a pair of points, she made her first assist on a pass to Ryla Jones, who made a smooth swing to put Penn State up 4-2.

Coming off a 12-kill outing against SMU on Thursday, Whitney Lauenstein got her first of the match on another assist from Stucky before Kennedy Martin got on the board to follow.

After beginning her career with Nebraska and Texas, Lauenstein was impressed by Saturday’s raucous crowd during her first time playing in front of them.

“I think they bring a lot of energy and it's a lot of fun,” Lauenstein said. “I'd love to see them at 10 a.m. tomorrow. It's definitely fun to be on the same side as them. I’ve played against them, but it feels good to be with them rooting for you this time.”

UConn won back-to-back points, but the blue and white responded with three of their own, forcing head coach Ellen Herman-Kimball to call her first timeout with the Huskies down 10-5.

It didn’t do much. Penn State rattled off three more points on an ace from Haley Burgdorf and kills from Stucky and Lauenstein to cap a 6-0 run. UConn finally ended the stretch when Maja Daca made a kill to cut the Nittany Lion lead to seven.

Schumacher-Cawley made the choice to start Burgdorf in her first home game, and it paid off. She made six kills on a .346% clip and posted six digs, all while only finding out she’d be in the starting lineup during warmups.

“I think sometimes I'll come out nervous, but I do try to hide it kind of well,” Burgdorf said. “But after a couple points, I'm ready to get after it and win the game. Just being calm and collected is my strong suit, and relying on my teammates that they’ve got my back.”

The blue and white won two of the next three points heading into the media timeout, highlighted by Lauenstein’s third kill of the set off Stucky’s ninth assist.

Back-to-back action brought the Penn State lead to 17-9, before the Nittany Lions went on a 3-0 run that ended with a Lexi Gin service error. Stucky continued her strong Rec Hall opener with a quick flick over the net that gave Penn State a 22-12 advantage late in the set.

UConn didn’t go down easy in the first set, though. Freshman middle blocker Courtney Grayson rejected a powerful swing from Lauenstein and made a kill of her own to keep things interesting down the stretch, but a block from Martin and Jones clinched the set for Penn State.

Stucky’s set-opening serve went long, setting the tone for a stretch where the Huskies won three of four points. Penn State responded with a dominant five-point run to regain the lead.

After a challenge reversed what looked to be a Penn State point, Gabrielle Nichols answered with an emphatic spike to give her squad a 9-6 lead. This started a four-point run that also saw two attack errors and a kill from Stucky, resulting in another timeout from Herman-Kimball.

The longtime leader’s second respite shifted momentum, as the Huskies won eight of ten points to follow. UConn’s run brought the set level at 14-14 and led to Schumacher-Cawley’s first timeout.

Things stayed tight, but Penn State started to pull away on a four-point run highlighted by a dig from Martin that led to a Nichols kill. It wasn’t quite over yet, though.

Another late-set kill from Grayson and back-to-back aces cut Penn State’s lead to 22-21. However, Lauenstein and Martin fired off consecutive kills before a combined block by the Nittany Lions won them the second set.

UConn opened the third frame similarly to the set preceding it, taking a 3-2 lead early before a five-point run by Penn State saw the Nittany Lions jump out to a commanding 7-3 lead. UConn finally ended the scoring drought on a service error from libero Ava Faltudo.

Freshman middle blocker Kendall Northern notched her second kill of the match, before the Huskies won four of five points, tightening Penn State’s advantage to 9-8. UConn began a four-point run after that, taking a two-point lead before Lauenstein recorded a kill to end the stretch.

After another Lauenstein kill, Nichols won four consecutive points, making two kills and two blocks to help the Nittany Lions take a three-point lead. After a service error by Lauenstein, Finley Krystkowiak made the first three kills of her career to put Penn State on the verge of victory with a 19-14 lead.

Unlike the first two sets, UConn didn’t put up much of a fight in the closing stages. Penn State went on a three-point run to close within two of winning the match, and clinched the victory with a kill from Caroline Jurevicius to grab their first win of the year.

Up next

Penn State will play a doubleheader at Rec Hall against High Point and Hofstra on Sunday, with the matches set for 10 a.m. and 6 p.m., respectively. Both matchups can be streamed on B1G+.

title: 'I’m definitely coming back, Penn State' | DJ Diesel lit up LightsUP
author: Sarah Price | The Daily Collegian
description:
Students gathered on the HUB-Robeson Center’s lawn for Penn State’s annual free music festival, LightsUP Friday night in celebration of the first week of classes.

Run by the Student Programming Association (SPA) and Movin’ On as part of “Welcome Week,” the LightsUP festivities started at 5 p.m.

The event was free to attend, with special activities available to students around the HUB lawn such as face painting, henna, airbrush hats and even a mechanical surfboard. A Kona Ice truck also provided sweet shaved ice treats to cool attendees down.

Student performers, Waterfowl Festival Band and Spencer Graham kicked the night off and set the mood with some feel-good music, followed by DJ Flatman who played remixes of iconic songs like “Y.M.C.A.” by Village People.

According to Abby Wypych, the first few performers were enjoyable and quite impressive, especially considering they were students like herself.

“They (Waterfowl) surprised me because I saw it was student bands and I was like, ‘woah,’” Wypych, a third-year studying animal science, said.

After the student performers, Between Friends, a sibling duo, was the opening act for the highly anticipated headliner.

“It was really different from the DJing that was happening,” Naomi Michaels, a first-year studying kinesiology, said.

In the middle of their set, though, Between Friends left the stage due to a “We want Shaq,” chant circulating over a group in the crowd.

“Honestly, it was just super unexpected, but I guess they need to be respected too,” Lydia Laing, a first-year studying biomedical engineering, said in response to the duo's abrupt exit.

Michaels also commented on the sudden departure of the sibling duo, noting how confusing the situation was.

“I was surprised,” Michaels said. “I understood that it's disrespectful, but I feel like that’s just a part of entertainment.”

Shortly after Between Friends’ exit, DJ Diesel, widely known as Shaquille O’Neal, finally took the stage. Although he may be known more famously as a former NBA player for teams like the Los Angeles Lakers and the Orlando Magic, that didn't stop him from hyping up the crowd and playing his custom beats.

Unknown to many attendees, Shaq has been DJing under the name DJ Diesel since 2015.

“We didn’t know until we saw the advertisement for this, and we were like ‘who’s DJ Diesel?’” Wypych said.

Nonetheless, Penn State showed up ready to hear dubstep and electronic sounds on the HUB lawn from DJ Diesel.

Shaq’s large presence was felt immediately after he took the stage. Throughout his performance, numerous girls had the opportunity to be on stage with him, and he even had them sing a few lyrics.

“Put those phones away, it’s time to party,” Shaq said.

Shaq had the crowd singing along to his remixes of throwback songs such as “Livin’ on a Prayer” by Bon Jovi, “Don’t Stop Believin'” by Journey and “(I Just) Died in Your Arms” by Cutting Crew.

“I’m loving Shaq so far,” Olivia Bobber, a first-year in the Division of Undergraduate Studies, said. “I love his music, I love his mixes and it’s a really good vibe.”

Jackson Watters, a first-year studying finance, agreed with this sentiment and thoroughly enjoyed the 7-foot-1 celebrity's performance.

“I’m very excited about Shaq being here,” Watters said. “We’re vibing with it.”

The crowd was enthusiastic when Shaq remixed popular songs like “Mo Bamba” by Sheck Wes and “No Hands” by Waka Flocka Flame (feat. Wale & Roscoe Dash).

“I was not expecting to see this from Shaq, but I love to see it,” Janet Pajaziti, a first-year in the Division of Undergraduate Studies, said.

At one point, the Nittany Lion joined Shaq onstage during a remix of the song “Last Friday Night” by Katy Perry.

Shaq was enjoying Penn State just as much as the students, yelling “Ohio State sucks,” and even getting the crowd to chant it back. Toward the end of his set, Shaq even made a promise to students.

“I’m definitely coming back, Penn State,” Shaq said.

Despite all of the excitement and engagement from the crowd, DJ Diesel’s set ended unexpectedly due to technical issues. However, it was no doubt a night to remember for many who attended.

title: ‘It’s a special opportunity’ | Matt Campbell, Nittany Lions host 1st Victory Day at Penn State
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Blue Band, the cheer team, the Lionettes and the Nittany Lion all took the field to perform the regularly scheduled pregame festivities ahead of a Penn State game on Friday afternoon at Beaver Stadium.

However, the players themselves weren’t the stars of the show. This time, at Penn State’s first-annual Victory Day, underprivileged children with disabilities were given the opportunity to experience playing football, run drills and score a rushing touchdown.

True to the event’s name, the children even got to ring the Victory Bell at the end of the night.

“What a great night for our community, for our kids,” Matt Campbell said after Victory Day. “This world is about giving back and making a difference, and to be able to do that tonight, and be able to be with so many great families and young people that may never get the opportunity to play the game of football — it's a special opportunity for us.”

Campbell originally learned about Victory Day at a high school football camp in Michigan from Aaron Segedi, a coach at Trenton High School.

Since then, Campbell brought the event to his first head coaching job at Toledo, then popularized it at Iowa State before continuing it in Happy Valley.

Cooper Cousins, already beloved by the local community for his involvement with THON and Team IMPACT, a nonprofit organization that pairs an ill or disabled child with a collegiate athlete, said that the purpose of Victory Day “blends great” with the Penn State character.

“Why not do it on a night like this with the band, the cheer team, the Lionettes, the whole community around to give these kids an opportunity to feel what a touchdown feels like,” Cousins said. “It's not even just cool for them, it's cool for us to be able to experience something like that.”

Campbell emphasized how the event is about “putting things into perspective,” and said he believes that in the heat of the season, people can lose a sense of what is important to humanity.

Not only did Campbell claim the event was a great way to give back to the community, but also a way to give his players a night to “lean back on” as the team prepares for the season.

Victory Day was painted in the smiles and laughter of the children, their parents and the players that accompanied those families throughout the hour spent playing at Beaver Stadium.

“It's the best day of the year for me to get back to these kids to see a smile on their face,” Rocco Becht said. “It's truly the best thing in the world. As you can hear, it's the best day for them as well. We're just glad to be here and put a smile on these kids' faces.

As for the growth of the event at Penn State going forward, Campbell said that he doesn’t want the event to become a “popularity contest.” Instead, he wants the event to stay true to its goal of touching the lives of families in the community and grow naturally from there.

“This isn't trying to sell our program to anybody,” Campbell said. “This is to make a difference in the lives of other people, and to be honest with you, the more people we can make a difference in their lives, the better this opportunity is, and the more special this day becomes.”

title: Caden Grabfelder plays villain in return to Jeffrey Field as Penn State men’s soccer falls to Pitt
author: Elliott Inscho | Sports Editor
description:
Even after playing in 49 games over three seasons for Penn State, Caden Grabfelder was serenaded with chants of “traitor” by the Park Avenue Army as he entered the pitch in his return to Jeffrey Field.

The student section, featuring some members costumed as both a banana and cow, echoed the affront at the Pitt midfielder every time he absorbed a pass on Friday night.

Grabfelder had the last laugh. The senior midfielder converted a penalty to take the lead in the first half and spark the Panthers’ physical 2-1 victory.

“It was difficult, but at the end of the day we have to look at ourselves,” Amadou Kone, Penn State’s lone goalscorer, said. “We had some mistakes in the first half that we could have done better. Same thing in the second half. It's just about correcting those mistakes and going forward with that.”

The match got off to a pedestrian start until the sixth minute, when Kone beat his defender and seemed to have a lane towards the net, but was called for a foul after the referee deemed he pushed his opponent to the turf.

It was part of an early trend for the Nittany Lions, as they were called for five in the opening eight minutes, compared to Pitt’s none. The fifth, committed by Toby Grant, led to the best chance of the early minutes, as the Panthers’ free kick forced a punch from goaltender Daniel Peluffo-Wise.

Pitt upped the pressure on offense. Cannon Scretchen delivered a dangerous cross that was fired into Peluffo-Wise’s chest. Penn State got the Panthers out of their half, but the team from the east still controlled a lion’s share of possession as the 22-minute mark approached.

Penn State notched its first shot-on-goal of the match when Fielding won the ball off of Grabfelder and passed to Morgan Marshall, who fired a low drive towards the bottom-right corner of the net, but Pitt goaltender Jack Moxom pushed it away.

Moxom was called upon again when he punched away a long cross into the box, taking out Sheridan McNish in the process, to force associate head coach Brad Cole to sub him off for Nehan Hasan.

Cole served as the blue and white’s leader on Friday after head coach Rob Dow was shown a red card in Penn State’s preceding match against Missouri State.

“There's obviously an added responsibility,” Cole said on his role Friday night. “But every decision that we make is always discussed within the staff, and we had a plan coming in that we followed. [I] wasn't thinking about it too much.”

The Nittany Lions got another chance when Kone played Beckham Brown through with a lobbed ball. He sent it wide.

Pitt earned its penalty after the referee's initial no-call was overturned to a foul in the box.

Grabfelder grabbed the ball and stepped up to the penalty spot. A chorus of jeers rained down from a strong crowd in Happy Valley, but he remained composed and dinked his shot into the right side of the net.

After being heckled all evening, he returned fire to the student section, cupping his ear and rubbing the Pitt crest on his royal-blue jersey as he was engulfed by his teammates.

“They weren't creating high quality chances, and then obviously a penalty kind of changed the game,” Cole said. “We showed a lot of resilience to come back. At halftime, we were really happy with how things went. We thought we could pressure them a bit more, [and] in the second half we did.”

Penn State had a chance to answer back, as Grant McIntosh had space to shoot just outside the box, but he fired the ball directly into a defender.

Kone drew the Nittany Lions equal in the 38th minute, finding himself open and chipping a ball past Maxom. His second score and third goal involvement of the season inspired more offense from his squad, as they held possession in the attacking half in the minutes to follow.

“It's just my teammates putting me in positions to be successful,” Kone said about his early-season success. They have full trust in me, full confidence. They put me in the right positions, and it's just about me executing.”

Another almost-deadly chance came in the dying moments of the first half, when a ball delivered from nearly the midfield circle found McNish’s head, but he couldn’t deliver with sufficient enough power to find the nylon.

The second frame began similarly to the first, with both squads unable to get much going. Pitt midfielder Miguel Bertran took a long shot in the 53rd minute that sailed wide of the net.

Just over a minute later, Anders Bordoy fired a cross that took three deflections, two off Penn State players and the final off the post, before settling in the net. The score marked Bordoy’s first career goal and thrust the Panthers into the lead.

In the 63rd minute, Kone received the first card of the match, a yellow for pulling his opponent’s shirt. He won a foul in the 66th, but Brown’s ball towards goal bore no scoring chance.

Another yellow card was issued to Bertran in the 73rd minute, Pitt’s sixth foul in juxtaposition to No. 15 for the blue and white. On the ensuing free kick, the Nittany Lions delivered a ball into the box that caused some bodies to fall.

It warranted a challenge from Cole, but the reviewed video didn’t result in a penalty kick. Yet another yellow was delivered to Logan Oliver on a more harsh challenge from behind that might’ve been on another day.

As tensions continued to rise, Grabfelder saw a yellow card of his own in the 88th minute on yet another hard challenge by the Panthers. With just under ten minutes to play, there was a lengthy delay after midfielder Peter Doran went down with an injury.

Penn State’s fouls eclipsed 20 with less than five minutes to play in the match. With seconds draining from the clock, Grabfelder almost bagged a second goal with a curling shot on net, but Peluffo-Wise pushed it away at the last second.

The Nittany Lions crept past midfield and further into the offensive zone, and got a final scoring chance in the box, but Joseph Sheridan’s shot sailed wide to seal the defeat.

Up next

Penn State will stay home for another nonconference meeting, as they’ll face off with Bucknell on Tuesday. Kickoff is set for 7 p.m. from Jeffrey Field.

“We'll certainly be ready,” Cole said. “They also played Pittsburgh in their last match, so we've already watched them. They're a tough opponent, but we’ve just got to rest and rebound and have a good plan.”

title: Penn State urges community caution amid measles outbreak after 15 cases reported in Centre County
author: Neel Ved | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State officials issued a release on Thursday encouraging community members to exercise caution and take preventative steps against measles, a highly-contagious disease.

As of Friday, there were 460 reported measles cases in Pennsylvania this year, including two deaths, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health measles dashboard. These cases span 31 counties, with Centre County reporting 15 cases.

This week, Centre County’s reported cases were double the amount from last week.

According to the release, there are currently no confirmed cases at University Park or other Penn State campuses. However, 10 campuses are located in counties with confirmed cases.

Measles is spread through the air when an infected individual coughs or sneezes. The virus remains in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, though sometimes it can take up to 21 days.

The rash typically appears two to four days after the onset of fever. A person with measles is deemed contagious starting four days before through four days after the rash appears.

Penn State requires any incoming student to have two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination. Students are advised to contact UHS or their primary care provider if they’re unsure of their immunity status to learn more about vaccination opportunities.

If students believe they have developed measles symptoms or were exposed to the virus, they’re advised to call the UHS Advice Nurse at 814-865-4847, before going to the Student Health Center.

title: Penn State field hockey begins play under coach Hannah Prince, suffers overtime loss to No. 5 Virginia
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Hannah Prince will have to wait a little longer to get her first win as a member of the blue and white.

Penn State began its 2026 season, ushering in the coach Prince era in front of a sizable crowd against No. 5 Virginia. The blue and white ultimately couldn’t benefit from home turf, falling to the Cavaliers 4-3 in overtime.

Only 56 seconds in, the Nittany Lions fell behind for the first time under Prince. Penn State worked an early press off Virginia’s touch to start the game, and worked its opponent deep into its own half, but a deep-laid pass deflected off a blue and white stick, and worked past that effort.

With a majority of the defensive players out of position, Virginia passes easily found their way behind the defense for the Cavaliers’ Rylee Dennis to open the scoring.

The Nittany Lions’ fortunes improved from there despite Virginia holding possession in the shooting circle, with Hope Russo logging the first shot of the game for Penn State, but it aired over the net.

Penn State continued to press deep up the pitch, deploying extremely vocal play in its efforts, even including the phrase “Happy Valley” from players to dub one of its tactical switches. Still, after the first quarter, the blue and white trailed from the early leak in the defense with multiple long forward passes for the Nittany Lions without a receiver on the end of it.

The second quarter started with a much slower pace of play, as both sides were much more calculated and meticulous in possession. Penn State netminder Aby Deverka was forced to make her first save of the game roughly three minutes in, and her defense soon after failed to repay the favor.

At the five-minute mark, the Cavaliers found themselves with an odd-man rush, as Virginia played the ball to Riley Savage, who rocketed a shot with little to no chance of stopping.

The Nittany Lions regrouped after the goal and appeared reinvigorated, as they carried possession into Virginia’s half for the following minutes. The control allowed Josephine Purdy to fire a backhanded effort at the goal for Penn State’s second shot attempt, but it also skied the net.

With two minutes left in the half, the Nittany Lions threatened with a clear look off of a penalty corner. Still, the better of Ella Gaitan’s two shot attempts on the opportunity was denied on an acrobatic goalkeeping effort from Virginia. The Cavaliers utilized a much deeper rotation, using four more players over the half, with no field player playing the whole time. Prince, contrarily, used both Sienna Dunn and Morgan Snyder without a break.

Penn State started optimistically after the half, snuffed out the first Virginia attack with ease and countered with Dunn leading the charge, but the pass to Chloe Dhage went off her stick and out of play.

Just as the Nittany Lions’ missed chances began to stack, Virginia piled on via a rapid attack that netted a third goal courtesy of Livvy Barker. Last season’s leading scorer for the blue and white, Natalie Freeman soon after got her first attempt on goal of the game, but with a tight window on net she powered a shot that again missed the framework.

Penn State kept pushing, though. Russo again fired a shot at net, this time forcing a save, and a tight-strung pass in front of a point-blank Freeman in front of the net went offline, but the scoreless efforts kept the pressure up to end the quarter.

As time began to tick into the final quarter, the blue and white got more direct with its attacks, earning a penalty corner after three and a half minutes of play. The Nittany Lions’ efforts would finally be rewarded, as a deflection and scrum in front of the goal allowed Olivia Marthins to score an unassisted goal.

Crowding the shooting circle continued to be advantageous for Penn State, as Purdy soon cut in front of goal and played a pass to Gaitan that she converted, cutting the score to 3-2. Two minutes later, it would be tied, as Dunn dangled past the Cavaliers’ defenders to find Dhage for a dribbling tap-in.

With all going in Penn State’s favor, it had to deal with its first bit of major adversity in the quarter with a Virginia penalty corner with four minutes remaining. Still, Deverka padded away the shot attempt to keep it even.

The Cavaliers got another penalty corner opportunity, but a pair of stick deflections, the latter from Deverka on a heroic diving effort, saved the chance. The save didn’t stop the pressure, as another penalty corner resulted after a review, yet the effort into the circle was flubbed and Penn State took it into overtime.

The Nittany Lions threatened within the first minute of overtime when the Virginia netminder was forced to kick away a ball right at her feet, as the Penn State defense silenced the Cavaliers' early attacks.

That tide began to change as Virginia threatened with control and physicality, even knocking a pair of Nittany Lions to the ground briefly. That would be a sign of what was to come; the Cavaliers soon played a penalty corner to the edge of the circle to star Mia Abello, who fired a shot which found the back of the net to end the game.

Up Next

The Nittany Lions conclude their August competition with Sunday’s game against Lock Haven slated for noon.

title: Position preview | Penn State’s OL offers mixed bag of experience, youth
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s offensive line is a tale of two stories ahead of the 2026 season.

Only Anthony Donkoh, Trevor Buhr and Brock Riker have been starters for more than two games, while the other two players projected on the front five have not.

Here’s how Ryan Clanton’s offensive line is shaping up this season.

Returning starters

Of Penn State’s five projected starting offensive linemen, three of them are returning Nittany Lions from past seasons. But all three have varying experiences in Happy Valley.

Cooper Cousins was the first player to announce that he’d remain at Penn State in the wake of the Pinstripe Bowl, citing that playing for the university had always been his goal and that he’d stay loyal through it all.

Cousins is slated to start at right guard after spending the past two years seeing time on the field as a role player bouncing around the line. In his career, he’s made two starts — both last season — and only missed out on a single game due to injury.

Lining up next to him at right tackle, Donkoh has been considerably praised by Matt Campbell following his return from an undisclosed medical procedure that kept him off the field this spring, per Mark Brennan of 247Sports. The redshirt junior is the most experienced on the line in terms of starting games, making 21 starts in 28 games played.

“I have that experience and have the knowledge to be able to give back to them, and that's what I'm trying to do now,” Donkoh said on Aug. 7. “That's my role, trying to be able to give back, to be able to raise everybody up and get them up to speed before they have their you know first game time experience.

As the starting right tackle in 2024, Donkoh drew national attention despite suffering a season-ending injury against Minnesota in November, earning an All-Big Ten honorable mention and a spot as a semifinalist on the Shaun Alexander Freshman of the Year Award list.

Redshirt freshman Malachi Goodman has garnered a lot of attention throughout the offseason despite the fact that he hasn’t made his collegiate debut yet. He’s projected to protect Rocco Becht’s blindside at left tackle, inheriting the role from Drew Shelton.

Goodman, a former 4-star recruit, was Penn State’s top signee in the Class of 2025 after graduating high school as the No. 2 player out of New Jersey and the No. 9 offensive lineman in the nation, per 247Sports composite.

“Malachi, good news, is one of the most talented guys I've ever seen with my own two eyes,” offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser said in April.

Impactful transfers

The other two members of the potential starting lineup are transfers with different backgrounds.

Trevor Buhr, who’ll likely line up next to Goodman at left guard, is the sole projected starting Iowa State transfer on the line. He’s had meaningful starting experience with the Cyclones, making 12 starts in 21 games played. Last season, Buhr was named an All-Big 12 honorable mention.

Texas State transfer Brock Riker will likely round out the starting line at center. He had a standout redshirt freshman campaign with the Bobcats, starting all 12 games in 2025 and being named a second-team Freshman All-American by The Athletic.

Riker was one of the first players that stuck out to Campbell out of the transfer portal, he said on Tuesday, because of his experience with in-game reps. Additionally, Campbell noted that Riker has put on upwards of 30 pounds this offseason, reaching around the 305-pound mark, transforming his physique to play in the Big Ten.

“Not only (Riker’s) experience was positive, but the way he played,” Campbell said. “Then you research, man, he was great on the weightlifting team, he was a great wrestler. How he was built when he came, and we just felt like this guy's got a chance to be a really special football player.”

Battling positional depth

The most notable position battles at this point include the left tackle and the center spot, for which Campbell has expressed his excitement for the projected starters, but also emphasized that everyone is still in an “earn it position.”

At left tackle, redshirt sophomore Garrett Sexton and redshirt freshman Owen Aliciene are in the mix. Sexton is the more seasoned option, having appeared in all 13 games last year, while Aliciene only appeared in one during his true freshman season.

Redshirt senior Dominic Rulli — a former walk-on — is currently the projected backup center, having appeared in every game for the past three seasons on special teams. He made his first collegiate start at center in the Pinstripe Bowl.

Rulli was initially the favorite for the job, but part of the reason why Riker is now in the lead is due to an injury that forced Rulli to miss spring ball, giving Riker all of the first-team reps.

title: No. 10 Penn State women’s volleyball falls to No. 11 SMU in Spikes Under the Lights opener
author: Elliott Inscho | Sports Editor
description:
Penn State headed to Arlington to open its season in a high-profile exhibition tournament, and its time in AT&T Stadium ended in a way that’s all-too familiar for the Dallas Cowboys’ faithful.

Matched up against a No. 11 SMU squad that sat just a single slot below them in the AVCA preseason poll, the No. 10 Nittany Lions fell in a two-set sweep to open the year on the wrong foot.

After No. 1 Nebraska also defeated No. 17 Florida in two hotly-contested sets to begin the evening, it was finally time for the Nittany Lions to make their 2026 debut.

SMU started the exhibition off hot, winning back-to-back points before Whitney Lauenstein got Penn State on the board with a smooth tap that lobbed over the net and onto the jet-black court.

After the Mustangs got another point, Lauenstein received a pass from Kennedy Martin and powered the ball to the back line, barely landing in bounds. Alexis Stucky’s first ace in the blue and white brought things level at three points each.

The squads went back-and-forth to follow, tying again at 6-6 not long after. SMU capped a four-point run, going up a pair of points, but the blue and white scored two unanswered to tie things up yet again.

SMU led 11-9 at the media timeout, and won the next point before a service error finally got Penn State back on the board. After an already hot start, Lauenstein brought the blue and white back within one with an emphatic spike.

For the Mustangs, Favor Anyanwu showed off her vertical in the middle with several high-flying leaps that fueled the Mustangs to a 15-12 lead late in the set. Two back-to-back blocks from the Nittany Lions forced SMU coach Sam Erger to take her first timeout of the match.

It didn’t help. Martin and Ryla Jones combined to block a Suli Davis spike and tie the set, but Davis got her revenge by winning the next point to put the Mustangs back on top.

A serve from Anyanwu was too much for Ava Falduto and Emmi Sellman to handle, leading Katie Schumacher-Cawley to call her first timeout down 18-16.

Schumacher-Cawley’s timeout had a juxtaposing effect to Erger’s, though, as Kennedy Martin scored consecutive kills to knot things back up again. After an SMU point and a long rally, she notched her fifth kill to level things at 19.

SMU earned another point after a high-level dig from libero Victoria Harris to reach the brink of set point, but a service ace kept the Nittany Lions alive.

The Mustangs reached set point again, but Lauenstein delivered to extend it further. SMU got yet another set-clinching opportunity on a Penn State service error, but a kill from Martin lengthened things even further.

On their third set point, SMU nearly fell victim to Lauenstein again, but she fired the ball just wide to post her first attacking error of the set and give the Mustangs a 24-22 victory in the opening frame.

SMU kept its momentum to begin the second set, jumping out to a 5-2 advantage, but a lengthy review reversed the fifth point in favor of the Nittany Lions and made the lead just a single point. Anyanwu got her fourth kill of the match to put the Mustangs up by a trio of points, but Martin answered back with one of her own.

After two straight points won by Penn State, the squads traded the next few points before Penn State thought it’d tied things up, but another review reversed that call as well. Coming out of the media timeout, Davis notched a kill to give the Mustangs a 12-10 lead.

SMU went up by three as the set continued on, but Haley Burgdorf finished a kill on a fourth-consecutive assist from Stucky, keeping things tight down the stretch.

The match’s competitiveness was a theme throughout, and the teams found themselves tied again at 15. Lauenstein’s tenth kill gave Penn State its first lead since the opening set and capped a 5-1 run before SMU drew level on the next point.

Davis reached double-digit kills to force another timeout from Schumacher-Cawley with the Mustangs holding an 18-17 advantage. Lauenstein was sharp all night, but an attack error put SMU on the brink of victory.

Martin fired a ball past the back line to inhibit match point, and it seemed as if Lauenstein did the same on the next point, but a review further extended the match. In SMU’s second attempt to end it, Davis made no mistake and delivered a strong swing to send Penn State home early.

Up Next

Penn State will return to Happy Valley, where it officially begins the regular season against UConn as part of the Penn State Invitational. First serve is set for 4 p.m. at Rec Hall, with free t-shirts waiting for the first 500 students through the doors.
